author: Mike Ludwig
title: Ahead of Midterms, Tenants Call Trump’s Housing Policy a “Catastrophic Failure”
content:
Housing justice advocates say new policy proposals would empower landlords while squeezing already struggling tenants.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

As voters facing rising living costs head to the midterm polls, the nation’s largest federation of tenant unions has released a damning report on the Trump administration’s “catastrophic failure” to rein in greedy landlords and address a housing crisis that threatens to displace millions of working people from their homes.

In fact, housing justice advocates say the few housing policies proposed by officials working under President Donald Trump — a billionaire who inherited a family real estate business that was accused of discriminating against Black families in the 1970s — would further empower landlords while squeezing already struggling tenants.

The United States faces a shortage of 7.1 million housing units that low-income renters can actually afford, according to The State of the Nation’s Tenants, a report released by the Tenant Union Federation (TUF) on October 26. After years of inflation, the median rent for a one-bedroom apartment is $1,572 across the 50 largest metro areas. With the federal minimum wage stuck at $7.25 an hour, the average minimum wage worker must work 116 hours per week to pay for a modest two-bedroom apartment..

Additionally, zero states or major cities in the U.S. even have an adequate housing supply to meet the needs of lower-income residents. From 2014 to 2024, developers primarily constructed luxury rentals, and the number of units renting for less than $1,000 per month dropped by 9.3 million. The nation’s chronic shortage of truly affordable housing is a major driver of poverty, according to Pew Research.

“The breaking point is in the rearview mirror. The breaking point was many years ago for some of the tenants we are talking about,” said TUF Founder and Director Tara Raghuveer in an interview.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has moved to gut protections for low-income renters living in federally subsidized housing to make it much easier for landlords to evict people. The administration has also put forth a proposal to eliminate housing support for mixed-status immigrant families. Along with disasters such as floods and wildfires, evictions are the major driver of homelessness in the U.S., which increased by 33 percent from 2020 to 2024, according to the John Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Along with disasters such as floods and wildfires, evictions are the major driver of homelessness in the U.S., which increased by 33 percent from 2020 to 2024.

“The administration is hoping to distract the public from its inability to solve the affordable housing crisis by blaming scapegoats, and one of those is immigrants,” Hannah Adams, a senior attorney for the National Housing Law Project, told Truthout. “Rather than solve the housing crisis, or deal with the fact that everything is too expensive for working families right now, they are just trying to kick people out of affordable housing.”

Raghuveer said she frequently talks with people who work multiple jobs but are unable to make rent and stay housed due to a combination of inflation and a predatory housing market that Congress and the White House have failed to regulate.

“People don’t know where they are going to turn to next. The only options available to them are their car, an extended-stay hotel, or the street,” Raghuveer told Truthout.

Democrats and liberals have increasingly focused on the housing supply, arguing that removing regulatory red tape to make it easier for developers to build would increase supply and drive down prices. That argument is famously at the heart of Abundance, a book published in March 2025 by journalists Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson. However, tenants organizing on the ground see big holes in that framework.

“Why is ‘abundance’ the dominant idea? It’s because it benefits the very same profiteers for us to believe that the only solution to this crisis is to put more money in their pockets to build more housing,” Raghuveer said.

Instead of looking at the housing market in terms of simple supply and demand, Raghuveer said policy makers must address the number of affordable units lost each year due to an unregulated market. Developers and landlords consistently refuse to build affordable rental homes unless incentivized by public funding. When it comes to public housing in particular, Congress also provides subsidies, such as the Public Housing Operating Fund for building maintenance and other costs without holding landlords to account for living conditions and unfair evictions.

According to Raghuveer, this focus on building more supply at the exclusion of regulations makes little sense to people organizing tenant unions to challenge abusive landlords in communities beyond the hyper-wealthy and highly regulated metro areas of New York City and San Francisco.

“The story we have been told by mainstream economists is that this is a crisis of under-production, but that is not true,” Raghuveer said. “We have been building a lot of multifamily housing in the last several years … but it’s under-regulated. We are not preserving the truly affordable housing supply that already exists, and failing by not regulating the landlords who hike rents and displace tenants willy-nilly.”

From 2014 to 2024, the number of rental units that cost more than $2,000 a month increased by 5.8 million while the number of units costing less than $1,000 fell by more than 9 million, according to TUF’s report. Meanwhile, corporate landlords have gobbled up rental properties and colluded to raise rents. Private equity firms have acquired 1.4 million rental units since 2018. Data from the National Multifamily Housing Council show that the top 50 U.S. landlord firms now control 2.5 million units nationally.

Kenny Loth, a member of Tacoma Tenants and Newcastle Tenant Union in Washington State, said he has experienced homelessness in the past and knows what it feels like when “someone else holds all the power over your home.” As prices rise, landlords across the country are raising rents on tenants in buildings they fail to maintain, Loth said, pointing to his own “ultrawealthy slumlord” in Tacoma. After 90 percent of his fellow tenants agreed to form a union at the apartment building, Loth said the landlord retaliated by raising rents.

Now, voters in Tacoma are preparing to vote on a citywide ballot question that would allow tenants to report landlords that violate a Tenant Bills of Rights that was approved by voters in 2023. Landlord and real estate groups have raised more than $590,000 to defeat the measure.

“We’ve got nothing left to give, and now a cabal of landlords wants to buy up Washington’s elections to serve their interests,” Loth told Truthout in an email. “That’s why we’re building tenant unions across the country. We’re done letting landlords decide the future for the tenant class.”

Federal and other subsidies provide incentives for developers and landlords to build housing for lower-income people — and also can offer an opening for lawmakers and regulators to put guardrails on how public money is spent. After all, funds not spent on upkeep and repairs can easily fall into a landlord’s pocket. However, lawmakers have largely failed to put those guardrails into place, particularly at the federal level, Raghuveer and Adams both said.

For example, Raghuveer said affordable housing programs in many cities provide subsidies for building affordable housing but require landlords to rent out only 10 percent of the new units at prices considered “affordable.” Less than 13 percent of new apartment buildings built since 2020 are fully restricted to only low-income tenants, according to the TUF report.

Under federal policy, housing is considered unaffordable when people pay more than 30 percent of their income. Thirty percent is a considerable chunk of a paycheck to spend on rent at a time when 60 percent of people with annual household incomes under $50,000 in the U.S. report living paycheck to paycheck due to inflation, wage stagnation, and other factors.

The federal government could further regulate real estate companies and landlords that benefit from public subsidies in order to improve housing conditions and push more affordable units into the market, but the Trump administration has gone in the opposite direction. For example, the Department of Housing and Urban Development is moving to revoke a federal rule that requires landlords to notify tenants about unpaid rent and other charges at least 30 days before an eviction. Industry groups representing landlords and corporate real estate have applauded the proposal.

When advocates sued to prevent the rule from taking effect after the Trump administration attempted to push it through without public comment in February, the National Apartment Association filed a brief in support of revoking the eviction protections, which were established under President Joe Biden.

“When you kick a bunch of people out of subsidized housing, they end up flooding the rental market and also burdening local governments, who need to figure out a place for them to live. And that burdens local shelters and medical establishments in addition to law enforcement,” Adams said. “So it does have a huge ripple effect.”

title: Far Right Influencer James O’Keefe Charged With Voter Fraud in Minnesota
content:
O’Keefe used a racist accent and wore what he dubbed “Muslim garb” in his failed attempt to expose “fraud.”

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Right-wing provocateur James O’Keefe is facing charges in Minnesota relating to his attempts to illegally register to vote as part of an online stunt that attempted but failed to expose flaws in the state’s registration process.

There are numerous methods of registering to vote in Minnesota. One process, called “vouching,” is used by people who don’t yet have proof of residence in the state. The person seeking to register to vote can get an individual who knows them to vouch for them by signing a document affirming that they live at the address listed.

The process doesn’t end there — the person who is attempting to register has to provide other forms of identity, including their driver’s license number or part of their Social Security number.

Vouching is considered a secure method of confirming a potential voter’s place of residence. It’s also rare, with the process being used in only about 0.6 percent of all registration applications.

author: Theia Chatelle
title: High Palestinian Turnout in Israeli Elections Came Down to Matters of Survival
content:
“We fear that if we do not get this government out of power, we will lose everything,” one Palestinian voter said.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Jaffa, Israel — Outside of Ahva Elementary School in Ajami, a historic Palestinian neighborhood just south of central Tel Aviv, the mood was defiant on October 27, the day of Israel’s national elections. “We fear that if we do not get this government out of power, we will lose everything,” one Palestinian voter told me after casting her ballot.

It came as no surprise that she, like most of the Palestinian citizens of Israel I interviewed on Election Day, asked not to be named. Since October 7, 2023, more than 400 Palestinian citizens of Israel have been investigated by police for “incitement,” often over social media posts, according to the legal rights group Adalah.

During the 1948 war, which Palestinians call the Nakba, most of Jaffa’s nearly 100,000 Palestinian residents fled or were expelled. The fewer than 4,000 who remained were concentrated in Ajami, fenced in with barbed wire, where they lived under Israeli military rule until 1949.

Just weeks ago, it was not clear that the parties most Palestinian citizens of Israel vote for would even appear on the ballot. In September, Israel’s Central Elections Committee, a body of party representatives, voted to disqualify both Arab parties — which are led by and draw most of their votes from Palestinian citizens of Israel — from running in the election. The Joint List is an alliance of three parties running together to clear the 3.25 percent threshold needed to enter the Knesset.

Hadash, a left-wing party with roots in Israel’s Communist Party, is the only one of the three with both Jewish and Palestinian members. Ta’al’s platform has historically focused on the rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel. Balad, a Palestinian nationalist party, calls for Israel to become a state of all its citizens, with equal rights for everyone.

The other party, running independently, is Ra’am, a conservative Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas, which in 2021 became the first Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition.

The two Arab parties were eventually reinstated and allowed to run in the Israeli election, but only after an appeal to Israel’s Supreme Court.

As Israelis vote to elect the country’s 26th parliament (Knesset), Palestinian voters in the Ajami neighborhood said Gaza was at the top of their minds. Just down the road is a public memorial displaying photos of some of the more than 20,000 children who have, according to a UN commission, been killed by the Israeli military in Gaza since October 7, 2023.

The memorial, at Hajj Kahil Square, has been torn down more than once. In May, according to Bokra, a Palestinian news site, two men, one of them carrying a rifle, ripped the photos from the walls. The next day, Jaffa residents put them back up and renamed the traffic circle the “Gaza Children’s Roundabout.” Police, who ultimately answer to Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s far right minister of national security, have also tried to stop protesters from displaying the images.

Whether or not to participate in Israel’s national elections has long been a fraught topic among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Whether or not to participate in Israel’s national elections has long been a fraught topic among Palestinian citizens of Israel. Some fear that voting in the election would lend legitimacy to a state that expelled most of their families in 1948 and maintains a military occupation over Palestinians in the West Bank, and that human rights groups say has committed genocide in Gaza; but others view it as their only way to gather power in the Knesset, especially more than three years after October 7.

An unprecedented wave of homicides in the community has also pushed many to the polls. At least 184 Palestinian citizens of Israel have been killed this year, putting 2026 on pace to surpass last year’s record of 252, according to the Abraham Initiatives. Police filed indictments in just 12 percent of homicides in Palestinian communities by June 2026, compared with a historic rate of indictments in 65 percent of cases involving homicides committed against Jewish Israelis.

On Israel’s Election Day, a recorded voice message went out to more than 1 million Palestinian voters from Sousan Sultan, whose sister Susan was killed in April 2025, and whose husband, Ziad, was murdered last August. “My sister was murdered, and she cannot vote in the election,” Sultan said in the recording, asking voters to cast their ballots in her sister’s name.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main challengers have all ruled out forming a coalition with the Arab parties, even as polls suggest the opposition may struggle to reach a majority without them. Throughout the campaign, Likud (Israel’s largest right-wing party) and its allies have made those parties a frequent target of their campaign ads, using Palestinian electoral power as a way to drum up turnout among anti-Palestinian blocs.

Some ads depict images of Palestinian political leaders, including Ahmad Tibi, who was an adviser to Yasser Arafat, alongside center-right politician Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party leads the opposition, proclaiming the choice is “the right” or “Palestine.”

In the Negev, the desert region in Israel’s south that is home to most of the country’s roughly 300,000 Bedouin citizens, many of whom identify as Palestinians, voter turnout has historically been low. But in this election, that appears to have completely shifted. In the Bedouin village of al-Atawneh, turnout had reached 64 percent by noon on the day of the election, the highest in the country, according to Central Elections Committee data. In the last election, it was 41 percent for the entire day.

“We are seeing record-breaking voter turnout in the Naqab [the Arabic name for the Negev] today for the Knesset elections, reaching unprecedented levels,” Huda Abu Obaid, advocacy coordinator with the Negev Coexistence Forum, told Truthout on Election Day. “However, right-wing groups are intentionally delaying the voting process, forcing voters to wait in excessively long lines.”

Many of the Negev’s Bedouin citizens live in villages the state does not recognize, which lack connection to the national water and electricity grids and where homes face demolition for being built without permits. Israeli authorities demolished a record 5,187 buildings in Bedouin communities in the Negev in 2024 alone, up from 3,283 the year before, according to the Negev Coexistence Forum.

Far right parties sent their own observers to polling stations in Palestinian communities, and rights groups reported long delays in the Galilee, in the north, and the Negev, both home to large Palestinian populations. The Central Elections Committee said it had found no evidence of systematic tampering and that polling stations would stay open past 10:00 pm for anyone still in line.

On Election Day in 2015, Netanyahu warned in a video that Palestinian voters were heading to the polls “in droves,” a message widely credited with driving a late surge in support for Likud. This year, he did it again, warning his base of high Palestinian turnout and claiming, without evidence, that his opponents were trying to steal the election.

With about 84 percent of all votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, no party bloc was close to reaching the 61-seat threshold required to form a majority in the Knesset. Netanyahu’s bloc was the largest, at 54 seats, but it was still down from 68 he held in the outgoing Knesset. Meanwhile, the opposition bloc (composed of all non-Arab parties running to unseat Netanyahu) won 49 seats. The Arab parties won a combined total of 17 seats, the most they have ever won in history. Turnout among Palestinian citizens reached an estimated 80 percent, breaking a record set in 1999, and surpassing the turnout rate among Jewish Israeli voters for the first time ever.

Jafar Farah, director of the Mossawa Center, a Haifa-based advocacy group for Arab citizens of Israel, cautioned against reading too much into the numbers. Farah was elected to the No. 2 spot on Hadash’s slate in May but withdrew in September. He said the rise in Palestinian turnout does not necessarily mean Palestinian citizens have renewed faith in the Israeli state or its institutions, or believe the ballot can end the military occupation of the West Bank (a theme in some of the Joint List’s campaign ads), or change conditions in Gaza. Instead, Farah said, many voters see casting a ballot as a form of “damage control.”

At least 184 Palestinian citizens of Israel have been killed this year.

“The increase in turnout projected in the 2026 polls, if it materializes, cannot automatically be interpreted as a return of trust in the Israeli establishment or in the Arab parties,” Farah said. “It may also reflect a growing sense of the need for political protection in conditions marked by uncertainty.”

A May poll by Tel Aviv University’s Moshe Dayan Center found that while more than 77 percent of Palestinian citizens of Israel want an Arab party in the next government, only 40 percent believe Jewish Israelis genuinely support a political partnership with them.

Netanyahu’s challengers offer little on the issues many Palestinian voters care about. Eisenkot’s party says it supports Jewish settlement wherever it is carried out legally and opposes a Palestinian state. Eisenkot himself has said anyone still thinking about a two-state solution after October 7 is “simply delusional.” Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the B’Yachad list, has ruled out ceding any land to what he calls Israel’s enemies, an apparent reference to a Palestinian state.

As of today, the math appears simple: Without the Joint List or Ra’am joining the coalition, the opposition appears to have no way to form a majority in the Knesset. Yet Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman, two right-wing opposition leaders, are still ruling out any government that relies on Arab parties, and Eisenkot has not dropped conditions for coalition partners that most Palestinian lawmakers are unlikely to accept.

Palestinian citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers to get the Netanyahu government out of power, but it remains to be seen whether the other opposition parties will join in their efforts.

author: Katheryn Houghton
title: Hospitals Nationwide Are Closing Intensive Care Units for Critically Ill Kids
content:
Pediatricians expect more cutbacks in the wake of federal Medicaid cuts.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Hospital units dedicated to treating the nation’s sickest kids are disappearing nationwide. In the past year alone, hospitals have closed pediatric intensive care units for critically ill kids in Montana, Oregon, and Missouri. Overnight hospital wings for kids have also shuttered in Illinois and California.

Depending on the hospital, pediatric units — which are separate from neonatal intensive care units — can serve patients ranging from a few weeks old to well into their teens or early adulthood. As hospitals look to cut costs, many are converting those beds into more services for newborns or adults. As a result, pediatric intensive care has become centralized in medical hubs, requiring critically ill children to travel farther for lifesaving care.

“You can’t expect that people will be fine if the next-closest children’s hospital is a flight away or an eight-hour drive,” said Elizabeth Mack, a pediatric critical care doctor and spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Hospitals cutting pediatric care tend to cite low patient volumes; it’s relatively rare for a child to need intensive care. It’s also hard to find doctors to treat those rare cases because the nation is short on pediatric subspecialists, who earn less than those focused on adults. Meanwhile, hospitals are often paid less to treat children than adults, and buying gear tailored to kids adds extra costs.

The gap in care is acute in rural places. Cutbacks are happening across community hospitals, whether owned by small nonprofits or massive private equity companies.

A recent analysis of pediatric inpatient units, hospital wings that provide overnight care, found they decreased by nearly 30% from 2008 to 2022 — down from 1,749 hospitals to 1,226. That left three-quarters of the hospitals without any pediatric inpatient services.

Medical researchers and organizations warn such gaps will widen due to cuts in federal Medicaid spending. The Trump administration has added administrative hurdles to access the low-cost health coverage and whittled down who qualifies. While those changes focus on adults, about half of the nation’s kids are covered by Medicaid or its related Children’s Health Insurance Program. Public aid researchers have said that when caretakers get tangled in paperwork, children can lose coverage.

Fewer people enrolled in Medicaid — adults or kids — means hospitals are about to see a financial hit.

Mack, who also works as a hospital consultant on patient quality, said cutting kids’ services for most hospitals is “a spreadsheet issue.”

“This is a very pricey endeavor, and it’s not sustainable,” Mack said. “There’s not a great answer here.”

Even without recent closures, many sick kids already travel long distances to obtain care.

When Darby Waldbillig’s toddler struggled to wake up one morning in 2022, Missoula was the Montana family’s closest pediatric critical care option — a 100-mile emergency flight from their home at the time in Helena, the state capital.

“Her face was swollen. She was drifting in and out of consciousness,” Waldbillig said.

Her nearly 2-year-old daughter, Siobhan, had bacterial meningitis, a life-threatening infection that swells tissue around the brain and spinal cord. Local emergency room workers started antibiotics before transferring her to Missoula’s Community Medical Center, where Siobhan spent more than a week in the pediatric intensive care unit — the same unit that closed this month.

“I firmly believe it’s because of those doctors that she lived,” Waldbillig said.

Whether Community Medical Center can still take cases like Siobhan’s depends on how sick a child becomes.

Greg Cook, the hospital’s CEO, said most kids who come in the door will still be able to stay for treatment. The difference is that the sickest kids — those in critical care who, for example, need a ventilator or continuous monitoring for a seizure — would be stabilized, then sent elsewhere.

“We made the decision to take care of the kids that we could absolutely take care of,” Cook said. “It’s about quality more than it is about the dollars.”

In a later email, hospital spokesperson Megan Condra said the decision was driven by low patient volumes and long-standing staffing challenges. “Our decision was not driven by concerns about the quality of care currently being provided,” she said.

Cook said the hospital hasn’t been able to recruit pediatric critical care doctors to live in Missoula since its last local pediatric critical care doctor retired eight years ago. Instead, specialists have been flying in on rotations. Cook said, on average, the hospital saw approximately two kids a month who needed intensive care when the decision to close the unit was made.

Cook estimated the unit’s closure will affect roughly 25 patients a year. The next-closest option in the state is Kalispell — a pediatric intensive care unit about 150 miles north of Missoula.

Not all hospitals are hurting in the same way.

Community Medical Center in Missoula is owned by for-profit Lifepoint Health, whose revenue is more than $10 billion a year, according to its website.

Cook said hospital leaders downgraded the unit after consulting with Lifepoint Health. “Asking Lifepoint to float the program” wouldn’t have solved its main issue, he said.

St. Vincent Medical Center, a Portland, Oregon, hospital that closed its pediatric intensive care unit last November, is part of Providence, a nonprofit health system operating across seven states. The latest financial records filed with the federal government show Providence Oregon had a more than $15 million shortfall as of 2024.

But St. Vincent, like Community Medical Center in Missoula, cited too few patients, not money, as the main reason for the unit’s closure. The four-bed unit was often empty, said St. Vincent Medical Center spokesperson Lisa Helderop.

Raj Basu is division chief of critical care medicine at the Ann and Robert H. Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago, a regional hub that can treat really sick kids. He said if hospitals take on complicated pediatric cases without the doctors or experience needed, they could put patients at risk.

Pediatricians have said some community hospitals have low pediatric volumes. The U.S. birth rate has declined. And doctors have gotten better at diagnosing and treating kids early, while the development of vaccines has reduced once-common hospitalizations. Better medicine means more kids are surviving complex illnesses that once were death sentences. So when kids do need critical care, Basu said, they can have far more complicated conditions that take a lot of expertise to treat.

With widening gaps in care, Basu said, doctors worry patients will get worse in the time it takes to reach a medical hub.

“From the front lines, there’s a creeping sense, a concern, that kids are showing up a little bit sicker,” Basu said. “I don’t know that we have enough data yet to prove that.”

Basu, who is also with the Society of Critical Care Medicine, said such medical organizations are exploring solutions — for example, specialty centers that work with community hospitals to establish regional training and protocols to transfer patients.

Other potential solutions are securing more federal funding to cover services in low-access places and raising Medicaid reimbursement rates, said Kenneth Michelson, lead author of the study on declining pediatric units. Michelson also directs emergency medicine research at Lurie Children’s Hospital.

“There’s a case to be made that we don’t need this capacity, but this can’t be viewed as a typical good that we get from, like, a grocery store,” Michelson said. “This is people’s lives, children’s lives. So I think it’s more of a national necessity.”

He said the disappearance of critical services seems to ripple into more routine care as pediatric services shift to medical hubs. For example, the number of hospitals performing appendectomies on a child — a common pediatric surgery — decreased by more than half from 2003 to 2022.

Regional centers could be overwhelmed, especially by spikes in demand. Michelson said that happened in 2022, when children’s hospitals were full.

“Small, community emergency departments were having to call 10, 15, 20 different hospitals to try to find a hospital that would accept a patient,” Michelson said. “That’s probably going to happen again.”

In some ways, he said, people who live in places like Missoula are lucky because Community Medical Center still provides most forms of pediatric care.

Lauren Wilson, a pediatrician at Community Medical Center, said the hospital maintains an intensive care unit for newborns and will still have inpatient pediatric services, emergency treatment, surgeons, therapists, and some subspecialists. Local doctors can consult with pediatric critical care specialists elsewhere to treat, stabilize, and transfer kids when needed.

“This is still the place I would take my child if they were sick and I was worried,” Wilson said.

author: Cleber Lourenço
title: Brazil’s Federal Police Probe US Companies’ Collusion With Bolsonaro’s Campaign
content:
The investigation’s main focus is on dealings involving an organization founded with the involvement of JD Vance.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

On Tuesday, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino ordered the Federal Police to investigate suspected foreign financing of Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign. Bolsonaro lost to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the runoff. The investigation will also need to determine whether any connection exists between political support for the senator and foreign interests in Brazil’s rare earth and strategic mineral resources.

Dino issued the 38 page ruling as part of ADPF 1178, a constitutional challenge originally filed by the Brazilian Mining Institute (Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração/Ibram). He ordered that an investigation be opened under the Supreme Court’s direct supervision, due to the possible involvement of members of Congress, whose parliamentary immunity can only be overridden in the nation’s highest court, in the alleged crimes under investigation.

The investigation’s main focus is on dealings involving Rockbridge Network, a U.S. organization founded with the involvement of Vice President J.D. Vance, along with Brazilian businessmen Tallis Gomes and Pedro Sang. The Federal Police must determine whether these dealings involved money, services or other economic benefits intended to help Bolsonaro’s campaign.

Investigators must also identify who was involved in the contacts between representatives of the American organization and Brazilian businessmen, and what purpose those contacts served.

Federal Police to Investigate Possible Link Between Campaign Support and Rare Earths

One of the most significant parts of the ruling is the suspicion that efforts to finance political activity may be tied to foreign economic interests in Brazilian mineral resources.

Dino explicitly ordered the Federal Police to investigate whether there is “concrete evidence linking the discussions over political financing to the reported economic interests in Brazilian rare earths and critical minerals.”

Dino also wants to determine who may have made any proposals, who they were directed to, and what might have been offered in return.

At stake are resources considered strategic for sectors including technology, energy and defense. In his ruling, Dino noted that these minerals belong to the federal government and that their extraction requires authorization or a concession from public authorities, as required by Brazil’s Constitution of 1988

If evidence emerges of negotiations involving rural land, the Federal Police must also determine whether there was an attempt to get around legal restrictions on foreign ownership of Brazilian land, including through the use of intermediaries.

Suspicions about Rockbridge first reached Brazil’s electoral courts through a complaint filed by Renan Santos, then a presidential candidate for the Missão party. The Workers’ Party later brought its own information about possible foreign financing operations to the Supreme Court.

Dino noted that the arguments presented by the two parties overlap.

Covert Advertising and Favoritism on Social Media

Another part of the investigation concerns paid promotion of content favorable to Bolsonaro by accounts based abroad, particularly posts that cited projections from Polymarket, a foreign prediction market platform barred from operating in Brazil.

According to the complaint filed by the Missão party, foreign accounts that normally didn’t cover Brazilian politics began running paid posts about Bolsonaro’s candidacy around the same time, citing estimates from that same platform.

The Federal Police must determine who paid for this content, where the money came from, and whether any Brazilian intermediaries were involved.

The ruling also addresses the role tech companies played during the campaign. Dino ordered an investigation into “intentional asymmetries and algorithmic manipulation” meant to help or hurt specific candidacies.

To support the order, Dino compiled documents from Meta’s Oversight Board, statements from United Nations experts, and a letter from U.S. lawmakers who pointed to possible inequalities in how Lula’s and Bolsonaro’s campaigns were treated.

Among the incidents cited were restrictions on boosting Lula’s posts on Instagram and improper recommendations of content linked to Bolsonaro.

Dino also cited an October 21 opinion from the Office of the Electoral Prosecutor General, which found that Meta had failed to comply with court orders, including requirements related to transparency around election ads and how its artificial intelligence tools function.

The ruling also references reporting from Intercept Brasil on payments from Bolsonaro’s campaign to Elytron, a company that offered an artificial intelligence system abroad for political influence operations. According to that reporting, the campaign recorded payments of $116,500 to the company, while the Liberal Party separately reported another $25,600.

Weighing all of this information together, Dino said the evidence points to “intensifying signs of foreign interference in the electoral process.”

Investigation Will Be Overseen by the Supreme Court

Along with ordering the investigation, Dino notified 10 federal agencies, including Abin, the Council for Financial Activities Control (Coaf), the Central Bank, the federal tax authority, the National Mining Agency and the Foreign Affairs Ministry, asking each to consider any action within its own authority.

Dino also drew on an Abin report identifying hidden financing of political groups, disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks as possible tools of foreign interference in Brazilian elections.

For Dino, the issue goes beyond foreign citizens expressing political opinions, which is protected as free speech. The problem arises when representatives of international organizations work to advance economic or institutional interests through actions meant to interfere in the election itself.

Under those circumstances, Dino said, there may be an “instrumentalization of political party activity in service of foreign interests.”

Although Dino denied the Workers’ Party’s request to join the case as a formal party, he acknowledged the relevance of the evidence presented and decided it would be more appropriate to investigate it through a separate proceeding.

The Federal Police must report the case number of the investigation to the Supreme Court. The investigation begins two days after Bolsonaro’s defeat and will aim to determine whether his contacts with foreign businessmen and organizations were limited to political and commercial exchanges, or whether they involved improper financing, covert advertising and economic interests in Brazil’s strategic resources.

So far, there is no confirmed evidence that Rockbridge illegally financed the campaign, or that any commitment was made to grant mineral rights in exchange for political support.

title: Supreme Court Bars Judges From Pausing Deportations While Appeals Are Decided
content:

The Supreme Court stripped immigration judges of the ability to pause certain deportation proceedings on Tuesday, declining to block a deal slammed as “egregious collusion” between the Justice Department and the state of Texas.

The unsigned order on Tuesday halts the practice known as “administrative closure,” which allows judges to pause deportation cases. The practice affects thousands of cases a year, and has been granted 360,000 times since 1990, according to statistics by the Executive Office for Immigration Review.

The procedure clears a judge’s dockets while other circumstances surrounding the migrant are resolved, including appeals of criminal cases or if they are seeking humanitarian protections or other legal status. It can also give some people relief in difficult circumstances, such as those who were the victims of certain crimes or children who were abused or abandoned.

Data has previously shown that most immigrants whose cases return to court after administrative closure are ultimately allowed to stay in the U.S.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Says He’ll Accept Midterm Results If He Deems Them “Honest”
content:
Trump has repeatedly — and baselessly — suggested that widespread voter fraud may play a role in this year’s races.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On Tuesday, President Donald Trump told reporters that he would only accept the results of the 2026 midterm elections if he felt they were “honest” — echoing statements he’s made in the past while peddling baseless claims of widespread voter fraud.

When asked by journalists if he would “respect” the results of the midterms, Trump indicated his response may depend on the elections’ outcome.

“I will, if they’re honest elections, yeah,” Trump said. He then walked away, seemingly to avoid follow-up questions.

Q: You'll respect the election results whatever happens?TRUMP: If they're honest elections(That's a no!)

Trump’s recent remarks echo other statements he’s made regarding election integrity.

In February, for example, he said that he would only accept the results of the midterms if he deemed them “honest.” If not, Trump added, then “something else has to happen.” The president didn’t elaborate on what he meant.

In the spring of 2024, Trump similarly said he’d only accept the 2024 election results “if everything’s honest,” saying that, if it wasn’t, he would “have to fight for the right of the country.” Trump ended up winning that race, but afterward made grandiose claims that he had won with a mandate, despite not winning a majority of the vote and having one of the narrowest Electoral College victories in U.S. history.

Trump has peddled baseless claims that widespread fraud has affected election results over the past decade, particularly in the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden. In that year’s race, Trump repeatedly indicated a reluctance to accept the pending results, stating in July of that year that he would “have to see” the results before accepting them.

Months later, when Biden won over Trump, the latter refused to accept the outcome, filing dozens of lawsuits and ranting online about supposed fraud he could never prove. He eventually invited his loyalists to Washington, D.C. on January 6, 2021, the day the Electoral College was set to be certified. Following Trump’s incendiary speech that morning, a mob of his followers attacked the Capitol building with Congress inside, delaying the certification of the election.

Trump has continued to sow doubts about elections, including the upcoming 2026 midterms, with his administration publishing questionable reports suggesting that tens of thousands of voters are registered illegally. He has pressured states to remove these residents from voter rolls, and has called for Republicans to “nationalize” elections based on his claims, despite constitutional restraints that place control of elections in the hands of states.

Trump’s most brazen attempt to interfere with this year’s elections took place in Alaska last week, when he ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to preemptively sue to block the state from certifying a U.S. Senate election if the incumbent Republican, a loyalist to the president, lost the race.

These and other actions and statements from Trump have sparked doubt among voters that he will accept the midterm results, especially if Democrats win one or both houses of Congress, which they are currently favored to do. A recent Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll found that 7 in 10 voters are not confident that Trump will respect the election outcomes.

Some observers have posited that Trump could be attempting to create just enough distrust among his base for Republicans to justify refusing to certify the midterm results. In one such scenario, GOP Speaker of the House Mike Johnson could replace the House Clerk, or pressure the current one, telling whoever is in that position that they must refuse to seat election winners due to supposed voter irregularities.

Election experts say that such a move would likely be illegal and blocked by the courts. But given Trump’s history — and Johnson’s willingness to block election winners from assuming office before — many are worried that partisan maneuvers by Republicans are within the realm of possibility.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Egypt Shutters Independent News Site Mada Masr and Detains Its Editor-in-Chief
content:
This “severe blow” to independent media is an “unprecedented escalation,” says a journalist who previously worked there.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

A court in Cairo has ordered the closure of the independent Egyptian news site Mada Masr. The court also ordered the site’s editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, to be detained until she pays a fine of over $50,000. She was convicted on charges of managing an unlicensed website. Mada Masr is “the flagship independent media outlet in Egypt and a pillar of independent media in the region,” says Sharif Abdel Kouddous of Drop Site News, who previously worked at Mada Masr. The independent outlet was founded in 2013 “in the midst of Egypt’s revolution and counterrevolution” and has “managed to survive all of those years in one of the most hostile media environments” in the world. Still, “what happened today is an unprecedented escalation” because Attalah and Mada Masr had never before been referred to trial.

Kouddous adds that the attack on Mada Masr comes less than a month after Egyptian authorities arrested an entire newsroom at the independent fact-checking outlet Matsadaash. They remain behind bars.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, broadcasting from Colorado State University in Fort Collins, with Nermeen Shaikh in New York.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: [We end] today’s show with breaking news from Egypt. A court in Cairo has ordered the closing of the independent news site Mada Masr. The court also ordered the site’s editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, to be detained until she pays a fine of over $50,000. She was convicted on charges of managing an unlicensed website. After the court’s ruling, Attalah was taken into custody.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re joined right now by Sharif Abdel Kouddous, the Middle East editor at Drop Site News, previously worked at Mada Masr in Egypt for four years as a journalist and editor.

Sharif, talk about the significance of this breaking news.

SHARIF ABDEL KOUDDOUS: Well, Amy, this is a dark day for journalism, not just in Egypt, but in the entire Arab world. Mada Masr is one of the last remaining independent media outlets reporting the news in Egypt. It’s really the flagship independent media outlet in Egypt and a pillar of independent media in the region.

It was founded in 2013 in the midst of Egypt’s revolution and counterrevolution. It’s managed to survive all of these years in one of the most hostile media environments for the media in the world. It’s had its journalists jailed, foreign staff deported. Its website has been blocked for nearly a decade. Their offices were raided by security forces. There are various forms of intimidation, and the threat of imprisonment is always there. Lina herself has been hauled before interrogation in numerous cases over the years.

But what happened today is an unprecedented escalation. This has never happened before. Lina Attalah or Mada Masr have never been referred to trial before. Then, barely a week, you know, after their being referred to trial, they hold a court session today, where Mada Masr’s defense lawyers are denied a request to even review the case file, that’s given to them in the moment. They’re supposed to review it right there on the spot and present their defense. The court then calls for a recess to deliberate the request, comes back into session, clears the entire courtroom of everyone except for Lina and her lawyer, and then fills it with plainclothes security guards and security officers. And then the court announces it’s rejected all the requests by the defense, including to submit any documentation or hear any witnesses. And the judge then appoints a lawyer for Lina, despite objections, of course. And then, after that, he just summarily reads out the conviction.

And the conviction is fining Lina Attalah herself, as editor-in-chief and co-founder of Mada Masr, to the maximum possible penalty, which is a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds, which translates to about $50,000, the closure — and the closure of Mada Masr, of the website, and the confiscation of its property. And then security personnel physically surrounded Lina, physically lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom. And she remains in custody now. Her lawyers and her colleagues are scrambling to gather the money to pay the 3 million pounds before the courthouse closes in just a few minutes from the time of this broadcast, so she doesn’t have to spend the night in custody.

But really, you know, the future of Mada and of independent media in Egypt has suffered a very severe blow today. And if there is not a lot of noise made about this by journalists around the world, her colleagues and by the power brokers that this authoritarian Egyptian government relies on to survive, including, of course, the United States — you know, Egypt’s the second-biggest recipient of U.S. foreign aid in the world — if there isn’t an uproar, then we may lose this crucial media outlet in Egypt and in the region.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Sharif, as you mentioned, of course, Mada Masr has come under attack by the state many, many times and in various ways, but this, as you said, is an unprecedented escalation. Why do you think this is happening now?

SHARIF ABDEL KOUDDOUS: It’s difficult to say why now. Let’s remember this is coming less than a month after Egypt authorities arrested an entire newsroom of Matsadaash, six people from — arrested the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, which is six journalists, threw them into prison, interrogated them, abused them and tortured them and forced them to record false confessions, and they remain behind bars. And that was allowed to happen. So, that was also an escalation.

It’s coming after Sisi, the president of Egypt, announced a bombshell last week, where he said, for the first time in Egyptian modern history, that he is not going to — he’s going to step down at the end of his term. Whether that happens in 2030, whether that happens or not, we don’t know. Not that it will be a democratic transition, but the fact that he will hand over power in some way.

It’s also coming as Egypt has, controversially, agreed to send its military to Saudi Arabia to, what they said was, defend against attacks by Ansar Allah and the Houthis in Yemen. It’s coming as Egypt held this big conference, you know, lauding its achievements over the past few years.

But it’s also coming as the world is on fire, and, you know, no one may be paying attention to what’s happening in Egypt and what’s happening to Mada Masr. You have elections around the world that are consequential, that have happened in Brazil and Serbia. You have an election today in Israel. You have the U.S. midterms next week. You have the genocide continuing in Gaza. You have a war raging between Ansar Allah and Saudi Arabia and all across the region.

And so, it’s also coming at a time, I think, when the authorities — they’ve been trying to close Mada for many years. When I was working there, they raided our offices and hauled Lina away in front of us, and the managing editor and Rana Mamdouh, a senior reporter, and tried to imprison them. And they had the case ready and everything. And it was only pressure from foreign governments that had them released, and from solidarity within Egypt, as well. But this may be the moment where they can close it down and get away with it.

AMY GOODMAN: Sharif, we have to leave it there, but we’ll continue to follow this. Sharif Abdel Kouddous, Middle East editor at Drop Site News, previously worked at Mada Masr in Egypt for four years as journalist and editor. To see our interviews with Lina Attalah, go to democracynow.org.

We have to end right now, and I want to thank the amazing student team here at Fort Collins, Colorado State University, at Rocky Mountain Student Media, CTV: Michael Urbaniak and Laila Duran and Hazel Canner and Calvin Masten and Devon Allen and, as well, Josh Middleton and Hana Shiro and Beth Ryan.

I’ll be appearing tonight at Colorado State University’s Democracy Summit with a screening of Steal This Story, Please! at 6:30 at the Lory Student Center Theatre, and it will be followed by a Q&A with the film’s director, Tia Lessin, as well as the moderator with us, Colorado State University President Amy Parsons. That does it for our show. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

author: Chris Walker
title: Alaska Officials Seek Dismissal of DOJ Suit Aiming to Block Election Results
content:
Officials have “taken significant steps to distinguish” two candidates with the same name on the ballot, they said.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On Monday, Alaska election officials filed a motion calling for the “immediate” dismissal of a lawsuit, brought forward last week by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), that seeks to invalidate the state’s U.S. Senate race if the Republican candidate loses.

The race features three main candidates. Democrat Mary Peltola is neck and neck in polls with incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R). Meanwhile, a third candidate, also named Dan Sullivan, is running as an independent.

Although the latter Sullivan maintains he is running a legitimate campaign, Alaska officials alleged that he was trying to cause confusion among voters and initially kept him off the ballot. However, the independent sued the state, and won the right to be included in the election after the state Supreme Court found that his candidacy was proper and legal.

Despite the independent already appearing on the primary election ballot and early voting for the general election already starting, the DOJ filed a lawsuit last Thursday, demanding that the state refuse to certify the results if the incumbent Sullivan loses (most likely to Peltola).

“It is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” the DOJ lawsuit said, adding that one of the conditions demonstrating the outcome could have been “impacted by voter confusion” is if “Senator Sullivan does not win the election.”

Democrats, including Peltola, responded to the suit by requesting it be fast-tracked and, eventually, for a judge to deem it unfounded, especially since elections are largely meant to be administered by the states without federal interference. Shortly after U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason approved fast-tracking the motion, Alaska election officials filed their own paperwork with the court, asking for the DOJ lawsuit to be dismissed outright.

The filing was submitted jointly by Carol Beecher, director of the Division of Elections, and the Elections Boards of the State of Alaska, as well as the State Ballot Counting Review Board for the state, collectively calling themselves “the Division.” The officials recognized the situation was a rare one, but argued that shouldn’t allow the federal government to preemptively intervene in the race’s outcome.

“Although Alaska faces an unusual situation in which two candidates for U.S. Senator share a first and last name, the Division has taken significant steps to distinguish them on the ballot so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which,” the Division’s filing stated, noting that there is a “lack of evidence of any problems (or indeed, any legal cause of action)” described in the DOJ’s lawsuit.

The federal government also “lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate,” the filing said.

The Division pointed out that it has taken steps to minimize confusion among voters, including differentiating the two Sullivans on the ballot by listing one as the incumbent Republican senator, and the other as the independent challenger. Both men also have their middle initials included to alert voters to the fact that they are different candidates.

Beyond those actions, the Division noted that Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system will ensure voters have the opportunity to pick both Sullivans, if one of the choices is their true preference over Peltola.

“If any Sullivan-supporting voter remains uncertain which Sullivan is which despite this clear differentiation on the ballot, the voter can ask for assistance from others or look up information about the candidates using a smart phone or an election pamphlet,” the Division stated. “And if the voter is still uncertain, Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system provides another solution: the voter can rank the Sullivans as his first and second choices. That way, if the voter’s first-ranked Sullivan is eliminated, his vote would transfer to the other Sullivan.”

“The Court should promptly dismiss the complaint with prejudice so that Alaska can proceed to administer its elections consistent with state and federal law and without unwarranted interference by the United States,” the Division’s filing concluded.

Beyond the unprecedented nature of preemptively calling for an election result to be dismissed, the DOJ’s filing was unusual in that President Donald Trump ordered it to happen. In previous years, the DOJ has tried to appear, at the very least, nominally independent from the president in its decision making process for filing lawsuits or criminally charging people, but that practice has been abandoned under this administration.

“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump bragged to reporters last week, regarding who decided to file the lawsuit against the state.

Answering questions about the lawsuit and other actions his department has taken, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated that he wouldn’t rule out disrupting the results of other states’ electoral contests.

“It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process,” Blanche told reporters on Thursday, but added the department could take such actions in a “doomsday scenario.”

“To say that there’s no circumstances that we would ever do that…of course, I’m not going to say that,” Blanche said.

author: Michael Arria
title: Poll Challenges Narrative That Michigan Democratic Voters Are Split on El-Sayed
content:
Ninety-five percent of Democrats say they’re voting for El-Sayed, and just 4 percent say they’re voting for Rogers.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In the final televised debate for Michigan’s Senate race, GOP candidate Mike Rogers used his closing remarks to claim that Jewish Democrats were supporting him because they view his Democratic opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, as “too extreme” on the subject of Israel.

“Jewish Democrats who are afraid for their children when their daughters can’t wear their Star of David walking across Michigan’s campus, these are real,” Rogers told the audience. “My opponent’s rhetoric, his vitriol, is having consequences.”

The idea that El-Sayed’s criticisms of Israel have alienated Jewish Democrats is certainly not limited to propaganda from the Rogers campaign. In recent weeks, multiple articles have used this very narrative as their thesis.

“Michigan Democrats at odds over Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed as November nears,” a Quartz headline declares.

“Questions about El-Sayed’s stance on Israel, accusations of antisemitism, and his campaign’s relationship with [left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan] Piker have kept the party’s attention away from its general-election opponent, Republican Mike Rogers,” insists the piece. “The divisions come as Michigan’s statehouse and governor’s races are also closely contested.”

Division was also the theme of an NPR piece claiming that Democrats were trying to “unify” before the midterms. The article asserts that “healing the fractures is proving complicated” and quotes multiple Democratic voters who express reservations about the candidate over Israel.

“Democrats are still struggling to unite behind El-Sayed after the primary exposed deep disagreements over Israel,” says PBS News.

CNN said a “ruptured” Democratic Party is “trying” to unite around the candidate.

The Detroit-based Super PAC TFM is attempting to ride this purported wave, spending nearly $6 million on ad campaigns connected to a “Democrats for Mike Rogers” effort.

​“We believe in the true spirit of the Democratic Party, always standing against hate and bigotry, no matter where it comes from, who it targets, or whether it is politically inconvenient or not,” reads the campaign’s website. “We believe every American deserves dignity, respect, and equal protection under the law.”

This past weekend, a planned “Democrats for Mike Rogers” rally in Pontiac, Michigan, drew almost no one.

The Bulwark’s Joe Perticone shared images of the event on Twitter, showing three people in an empty parking lot and one person operating a camera.

“When your astroturf campaign meets actual turf,” joked the liberal social media account MeidasTouch.

Source sends along photos of said “Democrats for Mike Rogers” rally, happening now… https://t.co/fWWnVnbXA8 pic.twitter.com/wxhlMWVQGU

The low turnout probably wasn’t a surprise to anyone who read a recent Marist survey of Michigan voters. Despite the media narrative detailing a massive split among Democratic voters, 95% of Democrats say they’re voting for El-Sayed, and just 4% say they’re voting for Rogers. 3% of Michigan Republicans actually say they’re voting for El-Sayed, but this minuscule number certainly hasn’t led to a host of stories about divisions within the GOP.

“The Democrats have a six-point advantage against the Republicans on the generic congressional ballot question among Michigan likely voters,” reads a write-up summarizing the poll’s findings. “That leads opens up to 10 points among registered voters, little changed from the nine-point lead the Democrats had in September. President Donald Trump’s approval rating is upside down in Michigan, and a plurality of likely voters express worry about their personal finances.”

If this is reality, why do many articles on the race tell the story of a divided party, and why do they rely primarily on testimony from rare voters to convey a wider trend?

Furthermore, why do so few of these pieces point out that Israel has grown deeply unpopular among Democratic voters and that El-Sayed’s positions are consistent with the vast majority of the base? An April 2026 Pew poll found that 80% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents held an unfavorable view of Israel, compared with 53% in 2022.

This framing goes well beyond El-Sayed. The idea that the Democratic Party is divided on Israel is a consistent theme in the mainstream press, despite the fact that voters are effectively aligned on the issue.

“There’s only one problem with the tensions,’ ‘divided,’ and ‘wedge issue’ framing: It is not supported by any polls,” wrote media critic Adam Johnson in The Intercept earlier this year. “The ‘divide,’ such as it is, is increasingly not among Democrats or even liberals; it is between the supermajority of Democratic Party voters and party leadership. While party leaders such as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, and big Democratic donors, are pro-Israel, actual Democratic voters have moved on from Israel with remarkable speed and consistency.”

The pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC recently announced that it would stop issuing endorsements or directly earmarking contributions to political candidates. The move comes less than five years after the organization began making such endorsements. The shift exposes a clear truth: voters view AIPAC as a toxic entity, and their public support is doing more to hurt candidates than help them.

This was clear during Michigan’s Democratic primary, when El-Sayed highlighted opponent Haley Stevens’s connections to the group. An August Axios report showed that Mike Rogers even expressed concerns about an AIPAC endorsement, although he has since publicly welcomed their help.

This all seems relevant to next week’s election or, at least, more relevant than a split that doesn’t exist.

author: Alexis Goldstein
title: As the AI Bubble Threatens to Burst, We Must Prepare to Fight a Big Tech Bailout
content:
As firms like CoreWeave and NVIDIA start to wobble, let’s demand that the public won’t be the one left holding the bag.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

AI data centers are unpopular for good reason: they drive up utility costs for communities, crowd out everything from schools to family farms, and they’re bad for our health. But these data centers are also a financial crisis in slow motion.

The AI ecosystem is built on mountains of debt taken on not only by tech firms like Meta (which borrowed a record-breaking $25 billion in late 2025 to fund the building of data centers), but also by the companies that lease data center space to the Big Tech firms. Many of these firms have spent far more than they have come close to earning in profits: One estimate puts tech industry spending to build data centers at $1.9 trillion, but less than half of that money has been made in revenue.

The financial markets are taking notice.

There’s been significant turmoil in the tech sector over the past month — and at one critical company in particular: CoreWeave.

CoreWeave used to be a Bitcoin mining firm called Atlantic Crypto, but it started to pivot to AI in 2019. CoreWeave leases space to Big Tech firms at data centers they build and maintain. CoreWeave has paid for most of its data centers by borrowing: it currently owes more than $51 billion to investors, including two of the most infamous financial firms: Magnetar and Blackstone, as documented by journalist Elizabeth Lopatto at The Verge.

CoreWeave’s troubles have been piling up: its stock lost a quarter of its value — a 25 percent drop — last week, then dropped another 10 percent on October 22. Bond investors are demanding more money if they’re going to take on the risk of buying CoreWeave debt, a sign the markets are worried about CoreWeave going bust. Investors used to be content to be paid 9.75 percent a year to loan CoreWeave money until 2031; now bond market investors won’t take that risk without being paid almost 15 percent in annual interest.

But perhaps the worst bit of news for CoreWeave is in the market’s falling confidence in its ability to survive, as measured by the cost of an instrument known as the credit default swap, which is essentially a bet that a company is going to go bankrupt (it’s also described as insurance against that company’s bankruptcy). The cost of buying a five-year-long credit default swap for CoreWeave has increased over 164 percent in the past year.

It’s not just CoreWeave facing trouble. One of the most significant companies in the AI ecosystem is NVIDIA, the graphics card maker, which, on September 28, spent $150 billion to buy back shares of its own stock from the overall market.

It was a record-breaking stock buyback — no other company in history had ever purchased that much of its own stock. One reason companies buy back their own stock is to artificially boost the stock price. Often the CEO’s compensation is tied to the price of the stock, and so the company purchases its own stock back to drive up the price, thus guaranteeing the CEO higher compensation.

The market sometimes perceives a stock buyback as a sign of confidence, reinforcing the idea that the company itself is underpriced. But in the case of NVIDIA, it seemed to be an indication that there’s nowhere higher to go, and the only way to raise the price of NVIDIA stock, which has been on a record tear, is to artificially boost it. Financial journalists have questioned NVIDIA’s ability to keep rocketing upward since late 2025. NVIDIA stock is down around 5 percent since this latest buyback.

AI has been sold to the general public as everything from a panacea to a danger to humanity to a roaring bull market, but it’s starting to look more like financial mania.

In late 2025, OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar caused a stir when she suggested the government should backstop AI firms like hers. Astra Taylor and Naomi Klein warned about the potential for an AI bailout in their new book End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, and propose a new disarmament movement.

To disarm the big tech bomb, including AI, the public needs to be on high alert — as AI firms start to visibly wobble, we need clear demands and firm commitments from our leaders that if it all comes crashing down, the public won’t be the one left holding the bag.

author: Tik Root
title: Long-Awaited Climate Change Case Finally Goes to Court in Canada
content:
The outcome could prove persuasive in other climate litigation or spur new cases.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Climate change gets a rare day in court as 15 Canadian youth accuse the federal government of violating their constitutional rights by failing to adequately address the country’s role in global warming. Although thousands of similar cases have been filed across the globe, legal experts said this long-awaited case is arguably the most consequential to reach trial.

The lawsuit is the latest in a yearslong campaign by young people who are using the courts to force elected officials to mitigate climate change. Like similar cases in the United States, including the landmark Held v. Montana, the plaintiffs in La Rose v. His Majesty the King argue that the government has violated their constitutional rights by allowing the crisis to continue.

Set in Vancouver, the proceedings are slated to last five weeks, with the 15 plaintiffs expected to testify alongside climate scientists and other experts. “It’s the chance for the young people to tell their story,” said Kelly Matheson, deputy director for global strategy at Our Children’s Trust, the nonprofit behind this case and many similar efforts around the world.

The outcome, while not precedent-setting outside of Canada, could prove persuasive in other climate litigation or spur new cases. “We found that some of the positive decisions from some countries have been inspirational in other countries,” said Michael Gerrard, faculty director of the Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “This trial will be closely watched.”

The case began in 2019, when the youth, six of whom identify as Indigenous, filed suit. They alleged, among other things, that by not doing enough to combat climate change, the government had violated Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees “the right to life, liberty, and security of the person.” They also argued that federal action breached their equality protections granted under Section 15 of the charter because, as young people, they will bear a disproportionate share of the impacts of the crisis.

The original lawsuit took aim at much of Canada’s approach to climate change. The plaintiffs argued that the government had allowed emissions to remain dangerously high, set targets that fell short of what scientists said was necessary to avoid the worst outcomes, repeatedly failed to meet those targets, and continued supporting the development and expansion of fossil fuels.

Although the government did not challenge the reality of climate change, its arguments included a claim that the accusations were overly broad and the lawsuit improperly asked the court to resolve a political matter. A federal judge agreed and dismissed the case without a trial in 2020. The plaintiffs appealed. In 2023, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal of the Section 15 claim but allowed the Section 7 arguments to proceed if the plaintiffs more specifically detailed the government conduct that violated their protected rights.

The plaintiffs amended their complaint to focus on the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act of 2021, which commits the country to achieving the law’s objectives by 2050, and the 2030 emissions reduction plan adopted under that law. They argue that the efforts don’t go far enough to avoid violating their charter rights in the context of climate change and that the government committed to the net-zero law.

“Increasingly, people across Canada and the world are seeing the direct impacts of climate change,” said Andrew Gage, a staff lawyer for West Coast Environment Law who has worked on this case alongside Our Children’s Trust. “The plaintiffs will have their day in court.”

The Canadian Department of Justice referred a request for comment to Environment and Climate Change Canada, which declined an interview request but provided a written statement to Grist. “Our commitment to net-zero by 2050 has not wavered, and we are implementing an ambitious climate agenda,” a spokesperson, Samantha Bayard, wrote in an email. “The Government of Canada respects the role of the courts, the right of Canadians to bring matters before the courts, and the important role that an independent judiciary plays in our democracy.”

All 15 youths, who were between the ages of 10 and 19 when the suit was filed, are expected to testify. They will be joined by expert witnesses in climate science, renewable energy, children’s health, and economics. Closing arguments are scheduled for February with a decision expected sometime in 2027, although an appeal could delay a resolution. Still, it is unusual for such a case to even be heard.

“Seldom has climate been put on trial,” said James May, an environmental law professor at Washburn University who isn’t involved in this case but has supported some of Our Children’s Trust’s past work. He estimated that more than 3,000 climate cases have been filed worldwide over the past few decades, but most never reached a courtroom. The Hawai’i state Department of Transportation, for example, settled a lawsuit filed by 13 young people and agreed to develop a plan to zero out emissions from the transportation sector by 2045. The landmark case Juliana v. the United States was dismissed after years of litigation, and the Supreme Court declined to consider it.

Held v. Montana was a rare exception. After a seven-day trial in 2023, a judge ruled that the state’s energy permitting policies violated the plaintiffs’ right to “a clean and healthful environment,” which is enshrined in the state constitution. The state Supreme Court upheld that decision in 2024.

A similar outcome in Vancouver could have implications in other British commonwealth countries and beyond, said Matheson. “These courts are looking to each other,” she said. “There is momentum building.”

But even if the plaintiffs don’t win, May considers the trial a victory even before it starts. “It could serve as a blueprint for how to do this elsewhere,” he said. “It has already succeeded.”

title: Immigrant’s Death in Abusive Georgia ICE Facility Reignites Call for Its Closure
content:
Luis Sandoval was detained in a Folkston ICE center, where a hunger strike has been ongoing for over 2 weeks.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

An immigrant detained at an ICE facility in Folkston, Georgia, died on Friday, reigniting calls for the facility to be shut down and an investigation into the center as it faces an ongoing hunger strike protesting abusive conditions.

Luis Sandoval, a 48-year-old from El Salvador, was found with a “ligature around his neck,” according to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). According to the agency, facility staff found Sandoval at 1:46 am, and began lifesaving procedures. But he was pronounced dead at 2:28 am.

Sandoval, who was being held in the D. Ray James facility near Folkston, is the 60th known person to die in ICE detention since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term. He had only been in the facility for 21 days, having been arrested by ICE and sent to the facility earlier this month.

The Georgia Bureau of Investigation said that it has been requested to conduct an investigation into Sandoval’s death, per The Guardian, and ICE said that his death is “under investigation,” though it didn’t specify by whom. In a statement about his death, ICE highlighted Sandoval’s alleged criminal history.
