title: Netanyahu Extends Assault on Hebron Ahead of Israel’s Elections
content:
Israeli forces have displaced over 3,000 Palestinians from their homes in the West Bank city of Hebron since Friday.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Over 3,000 Palestinians have been displaced from their homes in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron (Al-Khalil) since Friday, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu carries out collective punishment in a bid to shore up support ahead of Israel’s elections on Tuesday.

On Friday, after two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on an Israeli military checkpoint in Hebron, killing two Israeli soldiers, Netanyahu stated that he would “prepare for a full lockdown across all of Judea and Samaria,” using the Israeli term to encompass the West Bank.

The Israeli military quickly locked down the city of Hebron — the largest city in the West Bank and its economic capital — and destroyed the Farsh al-Hawa neighborhood, where the checkpoint was located. Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said he ordered the destruction in the neighborhood, and filmed himself in front of a building being demolished. The army went on to convert some Palestinian homes into military posts for its operation, and forced families in the Ein Deir Baha neighborhood to leave their homes at night on foot.

Israeli soldiers also besieged the Fawwar refugee camp in Hebron, blocking the camp’s entrance on Saturday to prevent any Palestinians from entering or leaving.

Nearly half of those displaced are babies and children under the age of 18, along with elderly people and pregnant women.

According to Haaretz, Israeli military Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir moved to end the military raid of Hebron on Saturday, stating that its objectives had been met. But Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz insisted that the military operation continue, expanding the displacement of residents and preventing those who had been displaced from returning home.

“These actions by the Israeli occupation are driven by the elections,” Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari, told Democracy Now! on Monday. “We are days, or even hours, away from the Israeli elections. Netanyahu and the radical ministers in his government are trying to win as many votes as possible from the settlers. The Israeli response is disproportionate, and there is no justification for these actions.”

Al-Jabari also said that Israel’s actions constituted collective punishment — a statement echoed by the UN.

On Tuesday, Israelis will head to the polls in the first Israeli election since before October 7, 2023 — and one that polls show is an extremely tight race between Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot. Though Netanyahu is the longest-standing Israeli prime minister, his candidacy has been shaken by his corruption trial and his failures on and after October 7.

Netanyahu’s disproportionate response is likely fueled by his desire to demonstrate his ability to wage violence against Palestinians ahead of the election, and to shore up additional votes.

Netanyahu has also reportedly been considering renewed attacks against Iran, likely for the same reason. On Sunday, he published a video warning Iran “and its allies” against interfering with Israel’s elections, saying: “You will suffer blows far stronger than you can imagine.”

Tamir Sorek, professor of Middle East History at Pennsylvania State University, told Truthout that Netanyahu’s actions are consistent with Israel’s long-standing settler-colonial violence and dispossession of Palestinians.

“But at the same time, in these particular circumstances, Netanyahu needs to put what is called the ‘security situation’ at the heart of public discussion,” he said.

Netanyahu “knows that if there are discussions about corruption, for example, or about the economic situation, he is vulnerable,” Sorek went on. But if he can create the feeling of “a security emergency … then he has a better chance to succeed in the elections.”

“So for him, escalating the dynamics everywhere — in the West Bank, in the Gaza Strip, in Iran — for him, it is an electoral advantage,” Sorek said.

The escalations are not likely to end on Tuesday, either — particularly given the fact that Israel’s political parties will need to form alliances to create a ruling coalition, which could take weeks.

“We are likely to see him pushing toward more escalations,” Sorek said. This is for two reasons, he explained: The first is to show the Israeli public that there is an emergency, and to insist that the opposition is not collaborating and that government handover should not happen under these circumstances.

The second reason is to push against the Israeli opposition forming an alliance with Palestinian political parties.

“Although the leaders of the opposition parties declared that they are not going to collaborate with the Arab parties, what we see in public opinion polls is that the vast majority of the voters of the opposition do support [forming a coalition with Palestinian political parties],” he said.

Netanyahu has “an interest in breaking up this opposition,” which is more easily done “if there is an emergency situation, if the Palestinians are perceived again as the major existential threat for Israelis.”

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Data Center Near Yellowstone River Would Cause “Irreparable Harm,” Activist Says
content:
The Northern Cheyenne Tribal Council voted to ban data centers, but the Apsáalooke have yet to take a position.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The Northern Cheyenne Tribal Council voted unanimously this October to ban data centers on tribal land in Montana. The ban follows a decision in August by the Fort Peck Tribes to bar officials from projects involving data center developers.

But Montana’s Tribes are now split. Next door to the Northern Cheyenne, the Apsáalooke, or Crow Tribe, has not taken an official position and remains open to hearing proposals from companies, according to Shane Doyle, an Apsáalooke tribal member and The Nature Conservancy’s Indigenous right relations director. Doyle grew up on the Crow Reservation and has consistently advocated for reciprocity with the land, rendering him a voice in the dissent, whether he intends to be or not.

The stakes are highest in Crow country. In the small city of Hardin, at the Crow Indian Reservation’s northern edge, a former cryptocurrency mine is being actively converted into an AI data center. About 14 miles northwest of the reservation, Texas-based Quantica Infrastructure plans to build its Big Sky campus on nearly eight square miles of ranchland near the town of Broadview, north of Billings, Montana’s most populous city. As it’s currently planned, the data center would rank among the largest data centers in the world. The Yellowstone River Valley is “the heart of the Crow Nation,” Doyle said.

Krystal Two Bulls, who is Oglala Lakota and Northern Cheyenne, has been tracking these data centers closely. As the executive director of Honor the Earth, a nonprofit tracking data centers on or near reservation lands, she takes an extensive view of history and geography when it comes to tribal land and AI developments.

“Broadview is still a traditional territory of the Northern Cheyenne and also the Crow,” she told Truthout. “It may not technically be on the reservation, but it definitely is still going to have an impact on the land and the people around it.”

The divide over data centers comes as developers eye Montana for its land, water, and power, and as Tribes test how far their sovereignty can actually reach. Bans like the Northern Cheyenne’s are enforceable on tribal land, said Matthew Fletcher, a University of Michigan Law professor and member of the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians. But tribal bans on off-reservation data centers that affect reservation waters are “unlikely to be enforceable,” Fletcher said, unless a tribe can show a very significant threat to its waters, enterprises, or citizens’ health.

Quantica has asked Northwestern Energy for more than 7,000 megawatts. The utility currently serves about 750 average megawatts, said Anne Hedges, executive director of the Montana Environmental Information Center. “We’ve never imagined something this massive,” she told Truthout. The company’s plan includes about 1,700 megawatts of gas generation, which alone would be more than the gas generated by all Montana’s existing gas plants combined.

The gas would affect more than just the rural Broadview community. A retired Billings pulmonologist modeled the air-quality impact of 1,700 megawatts using EPA tools, Hedges said, and found fine-particulate pollution spreading to communities east of the site, including the Crow, Northern Cheyenne, and Fort Peck reservations. “It’d be a disaster,” she said.

The Northern Cheyenne resolution, which passed by a vote of 8-0, covers all land on the reservation, says Melissa Lonebear, a Northern Cheyenne citizen and tribal council member. It quashes any extant or future data center discussions on their territory. (None are currently active.) “We have fought historically to preserve our land,” says Lonebear. “We have fought against coal development, coal bed methane, all these things.”

The Northern Cheyenne own nearly all of the land within their reservation, which makes the Tribe a target for developers looking for large, contiguous sites, Lonebear said. She added that the governor had remarked in a closed meeting with tribal leaders that big corporations were looking for land. “I almost felt like we would be targeted,” she said.

Fort Peck’s ban bars the tribal government, individuals, and entities from discussing proposals to build data centers on the tribe’s reservation. The tribe passed the ban after three companies approached the tribe about data center projects on tribal land, Tribal Chairman Floyd Azure told Montana Free Press. Azure had asked standard questions about the benefits to his community, and after learning about the required natural resources, he strongly rejected theirs and any future proposals. Azure did not respond to Truthout’s request for comment.

Tribal water rights in the state define what is available for development projects like data centers. Fort Peck and the Northern Cheyenne coordinate with state environmental agencies, such as Montana’s Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC), to enforce these rights. “Physical and legal water availability analysis are part of the water rights permitting process, as is an assessment of adverse effect to other water right,” Patricia Spencer, a DNRC spokesperson, told Truthout.

Water rights are set out in an agreement between a tribe and a state, and sometimes the federal government. Such an agreement limits the amount of water available to the tribe within the state’s overall supply, which is sourced from groundwater and rivers near and far. “The proposed datacenter in Hardin is located in a basin closed by the compact, and DNRC cannot process or grant an application for an appropriation of water within the Bighorn River Basin,” Spencer said in an email. “At this time, DNRC has not received any water rights applications or change applications tied to that facility.”

The Crow’s calculation also includes revenue, according to Lonebear. The Absaloka coal mine, which was long the Tribe’s marquee employer and profit source, shipped its last rail car of coal in 2024, the Billings Gazette reported. In August, a Senate committee advanced the Crow Revenue Act, a bill with full-throated support from Crow reservation chairman Frank White Clay that would give the Crow ownership of their coal, previously paternally managed by the Hope Family Trust. In exchange, the Hope family is offering federal coal reserves in Bill Mountains, which they’re anticipated to lease to Signal Peak Energy, whose customers are in Japan and South Korea. The Crow also plan to participate in the mining directly in the future.

The Absaloka coal mine reduced capacity and then halted production in April 2024 after losing its main client, Xcel Energy’s Sherburne County Generating Station (Sherco Plant), in Minnesota, which pivoted to cheaper, cleaner alternatives like natural gas. It’s a loss that left the Crow without a clear surrogate source of revenue.

“The Crow Tribe has decided to develop their coal… and so the rest of the world should not be in our way for that,” Conrad Stewart, energy director of the Crow Tribe, told Inside Climate News.

“We’re trying to always make sure that we protect our water, keep it clean, make sure there’s enough for the fish and for people to drink and use in the community … So I think a data center would conflict with that.”

Water is on everyone’s mind. “We’re trying to always make sure that we protect our water, keep it clean, make sure there’s enough for the fish and for people to drink and use in the community,” says Doyle. “So I think a data center would conflict with that, with all our values.”

Asked whether the Crow will follow suit on the ban, Two Bulls said she was “hopeful,” but added that she doesn’t think the Crow will “entertain a ban or even a moratorium,” citing her understanding that tribal leadership sees data centers as a way to replace declining coal revenue.

The Crow chairman and executive officers all declined requests for comment.

Water may be a forefront issue, but that may not be the same for tribal consultation. Without a federal permit, federal land, or federal money, the federal consultation duties don’t apply: Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, NEPA review, and the federal government’s consultation obligations to Tribes.

The Montana Department of Environmental Quality has a public comment period that closes October 29 on Quantica’s water well. The company hasn’t yet applied for a water right, according to the DNRC, and that application will come with its own public notice.

Asked whether Montana’s Department of Natural Resources and Conservation must notify or consult the Crow Tribe, DNRC spokesperson Patricia Spencer pointed to the general public notice process. “Public notice, including an opportunity for the public to comment and make objections, is a part of the water rights permitting process,” Spencer told Truthout. “The Crow Tribe–Montana Water Rights Compact would not have any bearing on an application near Broadview.”

Meanwhile, the Montana Public Service Commission is developing a large-load tariff for data centers. The state legislature is scheduled to convene in January 2027, with what Hedges describes as dozens of data center bills. No Native legislators sit on the energy committee drafting them, and at the same time she called the American Indian Caucus “a force to be reckoned with.”

“We do not anticipate the construction and operation of our Big Sky Campus will impact tribal lands or water rights,” a Big Sky Digital Infrastructure spokesperson told Truthout over email.

“If we put a project like this in around Yellowstone County, in that river valley, it’s gonna be an environmental impact similar to a coal mine, or something that’s gonna cause irreparable harm to the area. I think that’s why there’s so much opposition to it right now,” Doyle said.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Serbia’s Student-Led Movement Sweeps Strongman Aleksander Vučić Out of Power
content:
Students “changed our understanding of what’s politically possible for all of us,” says journalist Lela Vujanić.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Serbia’s longtime leader Aleksander Vučić has been swept out of power by a historic student-led opposition movement against Vučić’s right-wing Serbian Progressive Party. Candidates from the Student List, who are not students themselves but largely first-time politicians selected by student-led popular assemblies, won a majority of seats in Sunday’s parliamentary elections, marking a seismic shift in Serbian politics. Their victory comes two years into a student-led movement sparked by the collapse of a roof at a train station in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 people. The disaster became a focal point for anti-government protests over corruption, cronyism, political violence and democratic backsliding.

“Students really changed the whole political landscape of the country, and maybe even more important, they changed political imagination. They changed our understanding of what’s politically possible for all of us,” says journalist Lela Vujanić, who speaks to us from Belgrade about the groundbreaking elections. “This was a great democratic opening and democratic awakening, not only for the students, but for the rest of the country also.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman in Colorado, with Juan González in Chicago.

In Serbia, longtime nationalist leader Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat following elections Sunday in a contest that pitted Vučić and his right-wing party against a student-led movement that had weakened his hold on power after two years of anti-government protests. The student-led movement first rose up in November 2024 following the collapse of a roof at a train station in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 people. The disaster became a focal point for protests over government corruption, cronyism, political violence and democratic backsliding. President Vučić conceded defeat after early results showed the Student List poised to win more than 135 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with only 105 for Vučić’s party. The historic defeat marks the end of a 14-year rule and a seismic shift in Serbian politics.

Tens of thousands of residents flooded into the streets to celebrate following the concession.

SEJLA KIPIC: The feeling is surreal. I laughed. I cried. I screamed. I jumped. It’s just unbelievable. After so many years of this tyranny and dictatorship, we are finally free. And that’s — you cannot put it in words.

AMY GOODMAN: The candidates on the newly formed Student List aren’t students, but political newcomers including farmers, athletes, artists and little-known experts. Students traveled through rural areas on foot and on bicycle to speak directly with voters in rural areas — traditional strongholds of Vučić. This is Student List candidate Radomir Saičić.

RADOMIR SAIČIĆ: [translated] This is a victory of courage over fear, a victory over unrest. Serbia can and must be different. Thank you for every step, every hour, every sacrifice and for every moment you chose not to give up. Thank you to everyone who raised their voice, stood by one another and showed that the future of this country does not belong to a select few, but to all its citizens.

AMY GOODMAN: For more, we go to Belgrade, Serbia, where we’re joined by Lela Vujanić. She’s a journalist and media researcher covering both media and social movements.

Lela, welcome to Democracy Now! If you can talk about this stunning victory of the Student List movement and what Vučić represented, and the changes you think will happen as a result of something we’re seeing not only in Serbia, but student-led movements across Europe right now?

LELA VUJANIĆ: Hi, Amy. Thank you for having me. I was listening the Brazilian segment, and I’m super happy for Lula’s victory and for Brazilian people voting this way.

But, yes, we have something quite historic and extraordinary happening in Serbia, as you said. Yesterday, it was Election Day, parliamentary elections. And our mass civic, social movement, that’s led by Serbian students, was able — that lasts already for two years — was able not only to challenge Vučić and his ruling SNS party, but to win popular vote in a landslide victory, winning 52% of the votes.

What’s also important, that they campaigned individually, I mean, their electoral list called Student List. When I say “individually,” on the other hand, people of Serbia actually did the campaign and campaigned together with the students and with their Electoral List. What’s interesting, that students wiped out everybody else. Former established oppositional parties didn’t pass the electoral threshold, which is actually set very low in Serbia, around 3%. So, as you can see, this changes everything. In a way, students really changed the whole political landscape of the country, and maybe even more important, they changed political imagination. They changed our understanding of what’s politically possible for all of us.

People were celebrating throughout the night across Serbia and Belgrade. There was also a moment of disbelief, because only few people in Serbia yesterday would say that everything — that Vučić will — that everything will resolve peacefully. Most of the people even expected some sort of the state of emergency, election being rigged. So, everybody was quite surprised when the former president got on TV yesterday around 10 p.m. and said, “Yes, students won, and I acknowledge the results.”

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Lela, I wanted to ask you — the press has described the Student List movement as being leaderless. And could you talk about how it became organized and whether it is, in fact, leaderless?

LELA VUJANIĆ: Thank you. Great question. So, for Serbia, what happened yesterday, it’s extraordinary and historic for Serbia, but I think it’s quite extraordinary globally and that this Serbian case will be studied and researched in the years to come.

So, the movement really is horizontal. And from its beginning, it was based and organized through — we say in Serbian plenums, so popular assemblies, based on direct democracy principles. So, after the fall of the canopy, of newly rebuilt canopy of the train station, students demanded political accountability from political class in the country, and they occupied literally all faculties in the country, across all four university centers in Serbia. They organized based on direct democracy principles, made their decisions through deliberations on plenums, and actually spread the model throughout the country. And citizens also adopted the model and organized based on the same principles, organized in their locales. So, citizens run — and this is still active — popular assemblies in their neighborhoods and in their municipalities. So, yes, this was great, great democratic opening and democratic awakening, not only for the students, but for the rest of the country also.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And the impact of these election results on the rest of Europe, especially since Serbia for years has been one of the countries, I guess, closest to Russia of the European countries?

LELA VUJANIĆ: Yes, Serbia has a somewhat specific position. It’s not member of the EU. It’s for 12 years already a candidate country. It didn’t introduce sanctions to Russia. But you need to remember — and Serbia is no stranger to Democracy Now! Democracy Now! reported almost 30 years ago about this controversial NATO bombing of Yugoslavia. So, Serbia was under sanctions itself back then. And this is also the reason why people, Student List included, not only previous government, don’t want to introduce sanctions to Russian Federation. So, when I say “specific,” non-EU, non-NATO country, but trying to join European Union.

Regarding student programs and our future relations of Serbia with other countries and world powers, so, students said no sanctions to Russia. We continue negotiations with Europe. We continue our strategic partnerships with China. And what’s probably the most interesting, that we will not be complicit, or we will not contribute, or we will not participate in the systemic erasure of Palestinian people.

AMY GOODMAN: Speaking of Palestinian people, we turn next to the occupied West Bank. Lela Vujanić, we want to thank you for being with us, Serbian journalist and media researcher covering both media and social movements, joining us from Belgrade after the stunning victory of the Student List.

Coming up, we look at Israel’s escalating crackdown in the occupied West Bank ahead of Tuesday’s election in Israel that will determine whether Netanyahu remains prime minister. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Bear Witness, O World,” performed by the New York City Palestinian Youth Choir.

title: New Evidence Allegedly Ties Trump to 11 Sexual Assaults Related to Epstein
content:
A new report notes several patterns of conduct that Trump and Epstein shared in recruiting victims.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The House Judiciary Committee Democrats have released a trove of evidence regarding allegations of sexual assault, including a new rape allegation, against President Donald Trump in relation to Jeffrey Epstein that the lawmakers say has been deliberately covered up by the Department of Justice.

The 50-page report, released Monday, contains testimony from 11 women who either accuse Trump of rape or sexual assault or say that they had been offered to Trump for sex by Epstein or Ghislaine Maxwell, with most cases happening in the 1990s.

The accounts were pulled together through interviews conducted by the committee, as well as FBI records and the portion of the Epstein files that have been released; the evidence was cross-referenced for timelines and corroboration of testimony between alleged victims. In all, the evidence sharply contrasts Trump’s claims that he was merely an acquaintance of Epstein, and instead paints a picture of Trump as a serial sexual assault perpetrator who collaborated closely with Epstein to find and traffic victims.

“These women have spoken to investigators and, in some cases, testified under oath, yet Trump’s Justice Department has shut down investigations, deliberately withheld evidence and, through Todd Blanche, prevented Ghislaine Maxwell from discussing a survivor whose account implicated Trump,” said the committee’s ranking member, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland). “Trump’s Justice Department appears to be covering up these crimes to protect the President.”

Five women said that Trump raped or assaulted them while Epstein was present or was in his company, as detailed in the report. The report also reveals, for the first time, Trump’s alleged rape of Beatrice Keul, who has previously said that Trump groped her.

Keul said that she was recruited to attend the Donald J. Trump American Dream Pageant in November 1993, and was approached by Trump at an event in the Plaza Hotel, which he owned at the time. She says that her passport was taken away when she entered the pageant, and that Trump promised her favors, including saying that then-modelling agent Paolo Zampolli — who was recently fired from a high-level position within the State Department — would “take care” of obtaining a visa for Keul, who is from Switzerland.

The report notes that Trump promised Keul that he could get her admitted to New York University — a promise that Epstein often made “to lure in and then control his victims,” the report says.

After that conversation, Epstein approached her, introducing himself as “Don’s best friend.” As Trump looked on, Epstein also made promises to Keul, including that he would arrange for her to travel to Mar-a-Lago for a party. “You know I can take care of you. We organize many parties with Don,” Epstein allegedly told her. Keul says that Trump raped her later that day, after sending an associate to invite her to a hotel room for a meeting; she described the rape as “brutal.”

The report corroborates Keul and Trump’s meeting with accounts from other women who say that Trump and Epstein used the pageant as a “hunting ground” to prey upon women.

The Democrats also collate other assaults committed by Trump in relation to Epstein, including numerous occasions where Trump allegedly forcibly kissed or groped a girl or woman while Epstein was present, as well as compiled evidence on the alleged assaults of young girls like the case of “Katie Johnson.”

The report establishes several patterns of behavior by Trump and Epstein in relation to victims.

The report notes, for instance, that Trump called Keul several months after the alleged assault to reiterate his offer for favors. Similarly, Trump also sent a postcard to model Stacey Williams, who briefly dated Trump, several months after allegedly assaulting her in Epstein’s presence to invite her to Mar-a-Lago.

The report notes that Epstein had a practice of calling foreign models to visit them in Florida, and that: “Trump and Epstein seemed to share the same playbook for recruiting and abusing women, all the way down to the university they promised admission to and the timing of their follow-up phone calls.”

The Democrats also found that at least five women “related extremely similar facts regarding how Trump and Epstein were fiercely competitive in their pursuits of women and girls, and several related similar instances where Epstein showed off ‘his women’ to Trump but then reprimanded and punished them when Trump initiated or attempted to have sexual contact with them.”

author: Wendi C. Thomas
title: Man Who Spent Years Undermining Voters’ Interests May Win Newly Drawn District
content:
Tennessee congressional candidate Brent Taylor has taken steps to strip authority from elected local officials.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Not two weeks after the Tennessee legislature carved Memphis into three congressional districts this spring, in a move designed to eliminate Democratic representation, Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor made his electoral expectations clear in a photo posted on social media.

Taylor and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett, a fellow Republican, sat side by side on the U.S. Capitol steps. “My friend Tim Burchett showing me the dadgum ropes,” Taylor wrote in a Facebook post.

On May 7, the same day that the new districts were approved, Taylor had announced his bid to represent the redrawn Congressional District 9, which for more than four decades had stood as the state’s sole majority Black district. During that time, it covered mostly the Memphis area; it now stretches across half the state and is majority white.

Taylor, 58, already has a track record with many of the voters he is now seeking to represent in Washington, D. C.: In his nearly four years as a state senator, he has taken steps to strip authority from local officials elected by many of those same voters. With the backing of a Republican supermajority, Taylor, who is white, pushed through half a dozen laws that superseded the power and priorities of local politicians.

Around the country, state legislatures from both parties have used preemption laws to control local governments. That tactic has been embraced by Republican-dominated statehouses in recent years as a way to restrict the ability of Democratic-led cities to enact policies state leaders disagree with, including protections for civil rights, public health and workers.

Memphis has long struggled with high rates of violent crime that have begun to fall only in the last couple of years. This is where Taylor focused his legislative efforts. He led the charge to prohibit judges from considering a defendant’s ability to pay when making bail decisions. He has tried to oust Steve Mulroy, the first Democrat elected as Shelby County district attorney in 25 years, and pushed through legislation authorizing the state to review every decision made by his office. And he co-sponsored a law that voided the Memphis City Council’s ban on police stops for minor traffic infractions, which had been passed after the 2023 beating death of Black motorist Tyré Nichols.

The question of how to keep communities safe has drawn divergent political approaches in Memphis — from Mulroy’s focus on rehabilitation as part of his effort to lower violent crime, to Taylor’s emphasis on aggressive prosecution and incarceration. Those approaches can mean very different experiences for the people of Memphis, which makes up most of Shelby County. Some elected officials and criminal justice experts warn that the laws Taylor has championed will embolden police to detain drivers without justification and the criminal justice system to lock up more people for longer periods in the already overcrowded county jail, where more than 65 people have died since 2018.

“I think he’s very dangerous for Shelby County, and he’s going to be very dangerous for the Ninth District if he gets elected,” said former Shelby County General Sessions Court Judge Bill Anderson, referring to how Taylor’s policies could especially harm Black men. Anderson retired in May 2025 after clashing publicly with Taylor over bail reform measures. (Anderson supported them; Taylor opposed them.)

Taylor is favored to win because of redistricting by Tennessee Republicans after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in April made it harder to challenge gerrymandering that dilutes the Black vote. The Mississippi native, who lives in an antebellum-style mansion in a tiny and heavily white community east of Memphis, has loaned his congressional campaign $1.5 million. The candidate made millions after selling his funeral home businesses to a private equity firm.

Taylor’s opponent is state Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a 31-year-old Black Democrat who has taken a very different approach to what the district needs. Pearson has called for addressing the root causes of crime by improving schools and economic opportunities instead of a singular focus on incarceration. He first made national headlines for his role in stopping the construction of an oil pipeline in a Black Memphis neighborhood. He is also one of two Democratic legislators expelled by the Republican supermajority after leading a protest calling for gun control following a 2023 school shooting. With deep family roots in southwest Memphis, Pearson has positioned himself as the better fit for the historically Democratic Ninth Congressional District. He has also received support from national Democrats and has outraised Taylor in campaign donations.

Taylor, who declined to be interviewed for this story, has said that the laws he has championed prioritize public safety. He did not respond to detailed questions.

But John Pfaff, a professor at Fordham School of Law who has studied how state preemption laws impact prosecutors, said tough-on-crime laws like the ones Taylor helped pass have historically been “a form of social control against disliked minority groups” under the guise of public safety.

Non-urban voters, Pfaff said, “do feel, however incorrectly, sort of victimized by expanding civil rights” that urban voters choose. While these voters cannot cast ballots in city elections, he said, they have another path by which to exert power: “If the suburbs and rural areas control the governor’s mansion and the state legislature, they then can use their power there through preemption laws that finally tell Memphis what they want Memphis to do.”

In January 2023, the month Taylor took office, the nation was shaken by video of violent policing in Memphis.

A street surveillance camera and police body cameras captured what happened after undercover Memphis police officers pulled over 29-year-old Nichols just a few blocks from his mother’s home. For three minutes, officers repeatedly punched the unarmed man in the face, hit him with a baton and kicked him as he screamed for his mom. Nichols would die from his injuries in the hospital three days later.

After pressure from Nichols’ family and community organizers, the Memphis City Council unanimously passed an ordinance in April of that year barring police from pulling motorists over for minor traffic violations, such as a broken tail light, as a pretext for investigating an unrelated, more serious crime. Research shows that these stops are disproportionately used to detain Black drivers, undermine the public’s trust in police and create unnecessary police encounters that can turn deadly.

Taylor, who had been in the state Senate for a few months when the city ordinance passed, said it made the public less safe by limiting the potential for police to investigate more serious crimes. The next year, he and state Rep. John Gillespie, a Shelby County Republican, sponsored legislation that prohibited local government from curbing law enforcement’s ability to conduct traffic stops, effectively undoing Memphis’ ordinance.

Nichols’ mother, RowVaughn Wells, pleaded with lawmakers to drop the bill. Speaking on the Senate floor, Taylor responded, saying that as a funeral home director, he empathized with the Nichols’ family, but “we can’t let that empathy, Mr. Speaker, cloud our judgment in protecting 7 million Tennesseans.”

Taylor’s intervention suggests “that Memphis voters don’t know what their best interests are,” said Martavius Jones, who was chair of the Memphis City Council when the city ordinance passed. “What we were trying to do would not jeopardize the safety of anyone — not even in Memphis, but much less the rest of the population of Tennessee.”

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, told reporters before signing the law that no one should limit police in their enforcement methods and officers should be held accountable for their actions.

“I think what’s most important for us to remember is that we can give law enforcement tools,” Lee said, “but we’ve got to hold law enforcement to a standard of using those tools appropriately, where there’s an appropriate interaction with the public.”

Eight months after Tennessee lawmakers passed Taylor’s preemption bill, the U.S. Department of Justice released its investigation of the Memphis Police Department, finding that its aggressive traffic enforcement had harmed Memphians. The Justice Department recommended that the city limit the use of pretextual stops. Such police activity enabled the “regular use of excessive force with impunity” and unlawfully discriminated against Black residents, the Biden administration’s report said. When President Donald Trump took office in 2025, his Justice Department retracted those findings.

Over the last year, law enforcement has ramped up the use of such stops, especially in immigration enforcement, as Trump’s Memphis Safe Task Force — a collection of more than two dozen state and federal law enforcement agencies, including the National Guard — descended upon the city. Taylor supported the effort, testifying before the U.S. Senate days before it began that the task force would “succeed in doing the hard work to infiltrate gangs and arrest more routine criminals.”

Since his first year in the state Senate, Taylor had also been working to displace the decision-making authority of another locally elected office: district attorneys, especially Mulroy, one of Tennessee’s two Democratic county prosecutors. Taylor called him a “far-left zealot” who “has the potential to make the scourge of violent crime even worse.”

In 2023, Taylor sponsored a law that transferred the power to review certain death penalty cases from county prosecutors, who are elected, to the state attorney general, who is appointed by the state Supreme Court. While the law applied statewide, it disproportionately impacted Shelby County, where half of the state’s 40 death row prisoners were prosecuted. The law, Mulroy said at the time, “effectively disenfranchises the voters” who chose their district attorney.

Taylor would go on to further weaken Mulroy’s office following Trump’s 2025 deployment of his crime task force to Memphis. As arrests soared, Taylor worked to place the district attorney’s decisions under unprecedented scrutiny, saying he wanted to ensure that the prosecution of task force cases was as aggressive as the task force itself.

One new law, co-sponsored by Taylor, authorized the state attorney general to review every case that comes through Mulroy’s office, including those that stem from arrests made by Trump’s task force, “to ensure the proper administration of justice necessary to protect the safety of the community.” The dispositions of each case, along with bail recommendations, would be reported to legislative leaders.

Republican state Rep. Andrew Farmer, who introduced the bill in the House, noted that it is designed to ensure that “all crimes that deserve to be prosecuted are prosecuted.”

Mulroy is “just going to have to work harder and ensure that people are continuing to stay safe,” Farmer said on the House floor. “We want Memphis to continue on the path that it’s going — up.”

The state’s district attorneys general conference, led by Republican former District Attorney Stephen Crump, opposed an early version of the bill, which would have applied to district attorneys across the state, because it could lead prosecutors to second-guess their decisions. He dropped his objections after the bill was narrowed to apply to only Mulroy.

That law has another provision aimed at Mulroy as well: If he declines to prosecute specific categories of crime, the state attorney general can ask the state Supreme Court to intervene by installing a temporary district attorney who would then decide whether to prosecute. Taylor has long sought to limit Mulroy’s authority, and the provision would be a way to do so. Mulroy said the effect would be “an unelected shadow DA operating in parallel to the duly elected DA.”

“Prosecutorial discretion and prosecutorial independence is a key fundamental part of our criminal justice system,” Mulroy said. “It’s clear under both the text of the Tennessee constitution and Tennessee Supreme Court case law, and this bill does great violence to those principles.”

Taylor co-sponsored a second law, passed in May, that requires Mulroy’s office to report to the state and the U.S. Department of Justice within 10 business days every time it has entered into a plea deal, or dismissed or lowered the charges on a felony offense that resulted from a task force arrest.

“Memphis residents deserve confidence that the significant investments being made to combat violent crime are matched with accountability at every level of the justice system,” Gillespie, who co-sponsored the bill in the House, said at the time.

Taylor argued the reporting requirements were necessary to give the federal government an opportunity to prosecute cases Mulroy dismissed. In a post on X and a statement made before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee, he called Mulroy “the weak link” in the task force’s efforts. He’s also claimed, without evidence, that Mulroy refuses to prosecute crimes. In a rebuttal, Mulroy noted that more than 40,000 defendants are prosecuted by his office each year.

Mulroy has sued to stop both laws, claiming they are unconstitutional because they unfairly single out Shelby County and create an administrative burden. The lawsuit is pending in state court. Meanwhile, Mulroy has objected to his staff spending time on the reporting requirements, which he called “pointless busywork.”

Mulroy’s election in 2022 as the county’s first Democratic district attorney in more than two decades came on the heels of a year with a record number of homicides. But Republicans’ tough-on-crime approach had grown unpopular with voters, and Mulroy vowed to be an alternative. He promised to deprioritize the prosecution of low-level offenses such as marijuana possession and shoplifting; emphasize rehabilitation such as drug treatment, mental health counseling and job training; and establish a unit to examine the validity of convictions.

One of the people who campaigned for him was William Arnold, who had spent nearly seven years in state prison before his conviction was dismissed following examination by a Davidson County conviction review unit. The community organizer said he saw Mulroy’s candidacy as a way to “support someone who could help Memphians in a different way.”

To see Mulroy’s power being muted by Taylor is disheartening, Arnold said. But that is not surprising to him, given how the state legislature has long treated the predominantly Black city, including replacing the Memphis Shelby County Schools’ elected board with a state-appointed one.

Among the preemptive legislation Taylor has sponsored, a 2023 effort stood out: the dismantling of a bipartisan effort to ensure Shelby County’s bail practices did not discriminate against poor people, who are disproportionately Black.

Under state law, magistrates are to “impose the least onerous conditions” when deciding bail and should set bail “as low as the court determines is necessary” to assure the defendant returns to court. But in practice, hundreds of people were being detained at the Shelby County Jail simply because they couldn’t afford bail, according to Just City, a Memphis criminal justice reform organization, which along with the American Civil Liberties Union threatened to sue the county in 2021 for violating existing state law. Being jailed while awaiting trial can cause arrestees to lose jobs and child custody, the organizations argued.

In August 2022, the organizations and county officials — including Mulroy’s predecessor, Republican District Attorney Amy Weirich — agreed on a new bail order that included an “ability to pay” calculator.

That tool quickly drew Taylor’s ire, and by the following January he had co-sponsored a bill to kill it, characterizing the calculator in a Senate Judiciary Committee meeting as a way of “essentially asking defendants how much money they happen to have in their pocket so that they can make bail.”

The bill’s supporters said judges should prioritize public safety when deciding whether to release defendants. “There is blood running in the streets of Memphis today because they’re letting people out,” state Rep. William Lamberth, a Republican, said on the House floor.

State law requires judges, when setting bail, to consider several factors, including a defendant’s financial condition. And Josh Spickler, executive director of Just City, said that’s exactly what the tool helped judges do.

Under Taylor’s law, however, “the defendant’s ability to pay shall not be considered.”

“That tied our hands as judges,” Anderson, the former Shelby County judge, said in an interview.

A 2025 University of Memphis study found that the median bail amount increased after Taylor’s law took effect. And the law’s impact falls hardest on Black residents, Anderson said, because they are more likely to be low-income and make up a disproportionate share of Shelby County jail occupants.

“To those of us in the system, it’s obvious what he’s doing,” said Anderson, who resigned in 2025 with six years left of his eight-year term. “He called them reform acts, but they’re not reform.”

title: For Child Abuse Survivors Like Me, Prison Reactivates Familiar Trauma
content:
Prisons will continue to retraumatize survivors as long as society accepts control as care and punishment as protection.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The man in blue is yelling at me.

His voice slices the air before my mind can catch up. My body responds first — heart racing, shoulders tightening, breath shallow. I know this reaction intimately. It is older than this moment, older than this uniform. It lives in muscle memory, in skin, in a nervous system trained early to survive authority.

The man in blue is screaming commands, provoking my trauma and post-traumatic stress disorder, though he will never call it that. To him, this is procedure. Policy. Control. To my body, it is a return.

The man in blue is searching me.

His hands do not ask permission. They do not pause when my breath stutters or my knees lock. They move with confidence, backed by the state. I am reminded how I was touched as a child — how adults with power handled my body as if it belonged to them, as if consent were irrelevant. I am reminded how silence was demanded then, too.

The man in blue tells me when to bail, when to move, when to stop, when to stand still. His instructions echo older ones — less formal, more intimate, equally violating. I remember being taught how to perform, how to comply, how to disconnect from myself in order to endure.

The man in blue wakes me up by kicking my bed.

My body jerks awake before my mind does, flooded with fear. This is not the first time I have been startled out of sleep by a man who wanted control. As a child, nights were never safe. In prison, neither are mornings. There is no sanctuary here — only submission or punishment.

Prison does not create trauma in a vacuum. It activates it.

The man in blue is watching me.

Watching as I walk. Watching as I eat. Watching as I exist. Surveillance is constant, normalized, justified. When I was a child, being watched meant danger. In prison, it is framed as safety. My body does not know the difference.

The man in blue roughs me up and cuffs me while I am already down. My sobbing is muffled, ignored, treated as inconvenience. I am told to obey. I am told this is for my own good. I am told this is how order is maintained.

I have heard all of this before.

Prison does not create trauma in a vacuum. It activates it. For survivors of childhood abuse — especially sexual abuse — incarceration is not merely confinement. It is reenactment. Strip searches, body checks, constant surveillance, verbal degradation, forced compliance: These are not neutral practices. They mirror the dynamics of abuse with chilling precision.

The uniform changes, but the power imbalance does not.

In prison, authority is embodied. It has a voice, a posture, a right to touch, restrain, and command. The system does not ask what a body remembers. It does not care how trauma lives in the nervous system. It demands obedience anyway.

I was abused by men who were supposed to protect me — family members, trusted figures, authority disguised as care. They told me I was safe while they harmed me. They told me to be quiet. They told me to obey.

Later, the state told me the same things. The man in blue said he would protect me.

The lie landed the same way every time.

Incarceration relies on compliance. Compliance relies on fear. For trauma survivors, fear is already wired deep. Prison does not rehabilitate us — it exploits what was broken long before we arrived. Women and gender-nonconforming people are especially vulnerable. Many enter prison with extensive histories of physical and sexual violence. Yet carceral systems are not trauma-informed by design. They are trauma-producing.

Incarceration is not just about punishment. It is about power over bodies — especially bodies that have already been violated.

We are told that strip searches are about contraband. That restraints are about safety. That surveillance is about order. But when a system repeatedly violates bodies with known histories of abuse, intent becomes irrelevant. Impact is what matters.

And the impact is devastating. Nightmares intensify. Dissociation becomes survival. Panic attacks are disciplined as defiance. Emotional responses are written up as infractions. Survival instincts are punished.

This is not a failure of individual officers. It is a feature of the system.

The brutality and inhumanity of incarceration is not an abstract policy issue. It is a lived reality — one that seeps into the body, the psyche, the soul. And prisons are especially cruel to those who are already carrying wounds. The carceral state does not heal trauma. It weaponizes it.

For a long time, I believed the man in blue. I believed I was the problem. That my reactions were flaws. That my fear was weakness. That my pain was noncompliance.

It took writing to break that spell.

Naming the man in blue — seeing him not as protector but as continuation — was an act of resistance. Writing allowed me to separate my truth from the narrative imposed on me. It allowed me to say: This is not safety. This is control.

On paper, I could tell the truth my body already knew.

That truth is dangerous to the prison system. Because once survivors recognize the pattern, compliance fractures. Silence breaks. The uniform loses its invisibility.

That is why incarcerated voices matter. Not as confessions. Not as cautionary tales. But as testimony.

People who have been inside understand something the outside world often refuses to see: incarceration is not just about punishment. It is about power over bodies — especially bodies that have already been violated.

When the man in blue told me I was free, my demons and trauma still festered inside me. Freedom did not come from release papers or commands barked through steel doors. It came from reclaiming my voice. From telling the truth even when my hands shook.

I am not free because the state says I am.

I am free because I named the lie.

Prisons will continue to retraumatize survivors as long as society accepts control as care and punishment as protection. Writing like this exists to interrupt that acceptance.

I write so the world can no longer say it didn’t know.

The man in blue does not get the last word.

author: Maya Schenwar
title: Announcing the Winners of the 6th Annual Keeley Schenwar Memorial Essay Prize
content:
The prize honors the work of incarcerated and formerly incarcerated authors who are writing toward a more just world.

The prize honors the work of incarcerated and formerly incarcerated authors who are writing toward a more just world.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

As repression has escalated in so many realms of U.S. life over the past year and a half, we cannot allow ourselves to forget that nearly 2 million people in this country experience some of the most constant and brutal state repression, in the form of incarceration. Millions more are on probation, parole, electronic monitoring, or another form of non-institutional confinement that often leads straight back to incarceration. Meanwhile, 79 million people in this country live with a criminal record and all the barriers and obstacles that come with it, and nearly half of U.S. adults have an immediate family member who has been incarcerated. Too often, in moments of crisis and upheaval, attention turns away from the millions behind bars, and the many millions more who’ve been impacted by incarceration. We must uplift the stories of incarcerated and formerly incarcerated writers who are sharing their stories firsthand — and calling us to action.

Today, the Truthout Center for Grassroots Journalism is grateful to announce the winners of the sixth annual Keeley Schenwar Memorial Essay Prize. The prize, awarded to two formerly or currently incarcerated people for essays related to imprisonment or policing, is given in memory of my sister Keeley Schenwar (1990-2020), who was a devoted mother, daughter, sister, friend, writer, and advocate for incarcerated mothers. Each year, the selected essays share some of the spirit in which Keeley Schenwar moved through the world (and wrote her own work): a spirit of empathy, open-heartedness, and resistance. Each winner receives $3,000 and publication in Truthout. This year, we received 614 submissions — more than ever before — and each one shone a powerful light. We wish we could have chosen many more winners; selecting two is a near-impossible endeavor. We’re so grateful to everyone who trusted us to read their work, and to everyone who participated in the selection process. In addition to members of the Truthout team, we are very thankful for Joseph Peterson, who bottom-lined the program and correspondence process, and for our guest judge Colette Payne, a winner of the 2022 prize.

The 2026 winners of the Keeley Schenwar Memorial Essay Prize are Harlow Scott, author of “Cancer in Prison: A Death Sentence?” and Jazzy Mason, author of “For Child Abuse Survivors Like Me, Prison Reactivates Familiar Trauma.”

Harlow’s essay, “Cancer in Prison: A Death Sentence?” chronicles her diagnosis with colon cancer, 14 years into her prison sentence. She describes the medical neglect and abuse to which she’s been subjected — and the long-term deprivation of healthy food, safe conditions, and emotional well-being that makes incarcerated people more vulnerable to cancer. Guards shackled her in the hospital in the days after surgery, rendering it impossible to thoroughly clean her wounds. Returning to prison afterward, she was forced to ride in a vehicle meant for prison dogs. She must regularly drink water that has been deemed essentially unfit for human consumption. And yet, Harlow writes, “If I die today, I don’t want to be remembered as another number forgotten amongst the casualties of the prison system. I want to be remembered as a spontaneous shimmering light, dancing and free.”

Jazzy’s essay, “For Child Abuse Survivors Like Me, Prison Reactivates Familiar Trauma,” points to the way in which prison functions as sexual abuse, especially for those who survived such abuse before prison. She calls us to recognize the impact of this constant trauma reactivation for survivors behind bars. Jazzy writes, “For survivors of childhood abuse — especially sexual abuse — incarceration is not merely confinement. It is reenactment. Strip searches, body checks, constant surveillance, verbal degradation, forced compliance: these are not neutral practices. They mirror the dynamics of abuse with chilling precision.” Her essay also emanates a spirit of persistent resistance, which infuses every step of her struggle against the “man in blue.”

Both of this year’s prizewinning authors map their own stories onto a larger political analysis, one that recognizes the complicity of the entire carceral system in a web of interconnected violences. Taken together, these essays show us that, in this age of so-called “trauma-informed prisons” and “mental health jails,” prison is — by nature — not healing, rehabilitative, or safe. It is not trauma-informed; it is trauma. As Jazzy puts it, “That is why incarcerated voices matter. Not as confessions. Not as cautionary tales. But as testimony. People who have been inside understand something the outside world often refuses to see: Incarceration is not just about punishment. It is about power over bodies — especially bodies that have already been violated.”

I want to offer my deep congratulations to this year’s winners, and gratitude for sharing their stories and their insights with the world. Also, I’m extending a massive thank you to all who submitted essays, and to everyone writing against authoritarianism, surveillance, confinement, and carceral control. Your words inspire us and show us that there’s a path beyond these horrors.

The work of these writers points toward a future in which no one is an incarcerated writer — a future built on freedom, liberation, and autonomy, in which everyone has what they need to thrive. In the meantime, I’m drawing courage from Harlow Scott, who writes, “My life force remains. I won’t let them steal it, in the time I have left.”

title: Israel Launches Major Ethnic Cleansing Escalation in West Bank, Targeting Hebron
content:
The operation follows a Palestinian resistance attack on an illegal West Bank military checkpoint.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Israeli forces on Friday began demolishing homes and businesses and forcibly evacuating residents near Hebron in the illegally occupied West Bank following a Palestinian resistance attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.

“First, we will destroy this place and completely transform it, but we will do something that has never been done before,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the scene of the shooting attack that took place earlier Friday near Hebron Junction. “We will evacuate the residents, go from house to house, remove weapons from there as well, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure.”

“We will consider expanding this model to other cities as well,” Netanyahu added.

As expected, Israel kills Palestinians every day for months on end and nobody bats an eye; Palestinians finally respond, attacking Israeli soldiers at an Israeli military checkpoint on occupied Palestinian land, and its front page news and Israel makes the entire West Bank pay. https://t.co/iaSYIE7AML

The prime minister also ordered the Israeli military to “immediately impose a lockdown on Hebron and prepare for a full lockdown” of the entire West Bank, while vowing to launch the largest military operation in the occupied territory since it was conquered during the 1967 Six-Day War and subsequently ethnically cleansed of more than 100,000 Palestinians.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz also vowed that neighborhoods associated with the attackers would be “evacuated” — a word that critics call a euphemism for ethnic cleansing — “just like in Gaza; just like in Lebanon.”

Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich echoed those calls.

“There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons, and eliminate terrorists,” he said, referring to Israel’s name for the West Bank.

“Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon,” Smotrich added.

Israeli occupation forces are forcibly evacuating residents from their homes in preparation for demolishing them in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron. pic.twitter.com/KaDpsbVFNc

Israeli forces have killed or wounded more than 250,000 people in Gaza since the Hamas-led attack of October 2023, while forcibly displacing around 1.9 million residents and destroying or damaging more than 80% of the strip’s structures. In Lebanon, nearly 40,000 people have been killed or injured by Israeli attacks over the same period, during which there were two waves of mass displacement in which more than a million people were forced from their homes each time. Dozens of Lebanese villages have been flattened.

Demolition and displacement were the order of the day in the West Bank Friday as Israeli bulldozers began demolishing homes after Netanyahu’s announcement, even as local residents said their properties had no connection to the attack on the slain Israeli troops.

The Times of Israel reported that soldiers ordered Palestinians in the Farsh al-Hawa area to evacuate ahead of demolitions, with footage showing residents being pushed out as their belongings were loaded onto trucks.

“We are already here with the equipment on the ground, sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: If you mess with us, we will exact a very, very painful price from you,” Smotrich said in Farsh al-Hawa.

Israeli occupation forces begin a large-scale demolition operation near the site of a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers and injured others in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron. pic.twitter.com/H5DEHvMKbr

Israel’s High Court intervened and issued a temporary order to halt demolitions after Arab-Israeli human rights lawyer Mohammed Dahleh filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners who claimed the destruction violated Israeli law as well as international prohibitions on collective punishment.

“What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of the West Bank,” Dahleh told The Guardian. “They want to wipe out entire areas exactly as they did in Gaza and the refugee camps in the West Bank.”

Another Israeli human rights attorney, Michael Sfard, called Smotrich’s video announcement a “direct admission” of collective punishment.

The demolitions and forced evacuations are unfolding amid a wider Israeli campaign of home destruction, settler pogroms and other deadly violence, and displacement that Palestinian rights advocates and United Nations officials have called ethnic cleansing.

Palestinian olive harvesters, as well as international solidarity activists accompanying them, journalists covering settler attacks, and even international diplomats have come under attack by Israeli military-backed settler terrorists. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said earlier this week that between September 1 and October 12, Israeli settlers carried out 199 attacks connected to the harvest, killing one Palestinian, injuring 124, and damaging more than 2,500 trees and saplings.

According to OCHA, over 1,130 Palestinians — at least 250 of them children — have been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers in the West Bank since October 2023.

Friday’s developments came four days ahead of Israel’s elections, in which the ruling far-right coalition is trying to boost support among voters, including settler colonists pushing the government to annex the West Bank.

Netanyahu has vowed to annex all settler colonies. Smotrich has presented a plan to annex approximately 82% of the West Bank, excluding six major Palestinian cities. Ben-Gvir wants to annex the entire West Bank.

Israel’s actions on Friday drew widespread condemnation.

“Israeli leaders are publicly announcing plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes,” the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem said, while imploring “governments and international institutions to act now, using all means available under international law, to prevent the forcible displacement of Palestinian civilians, collective punishment, and extensive unlawful destruction in Hebron.”

author: Brooke Migdon
title: Ballot Measures Will Impact LGBTQ+ Rights in 7 States This Election
content:
Voters will decide how trans youth can participate in school sports, access gender-affirming health care, and more.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Voters in seven states this fall will weigh more than half a dozen ballot initiatives with direct bearings on LGBTQ+ people — disproportionately on transgender youth. They come as LGBTQ+ rights issues feature heavily in campaigns for candidates on either side of the aisle in the final stretch of November’s midterm elections, which will determine party control of Congress and several key governorships.

Nearly half of LGBTQ+-related ballot initiatives this year would restrict trans student-athletes from competing in line with their gender identity, an issue championed overwhelmingly by Republicans and by a rising share of Democrats. Others would ban certain transition-related treatments for minors — another focus of conservative candidates and President Donald Trump’s second administration.

Since 2021, more than half the nation has adopted laws barring trans students from playing on school sports teams matching their gender identity, and 27 states have banned gender-affirming care for trans youth. Nationally, the number of trans students who participate in school sports is unknown, but is believed to be relatively low: The Williams Institute estimates that just over 300,000 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States are trans, and not all of them will play sports.

In Washington state, where voters will decide this fall whether to ban trans student-athletes from teams matching their gender identity, the organization governing high school sports told The 19th that it is aware of about 10 trans middle and high schoolers who play sports out of more than 200,000 students who compete statewide.

Other ballot initiatives appearing before voters this fall include measures to change the state constitution to expand nondiscrimination protections for LGBTQ+ people; formally repeal language against same-sex marriages and modify students’ and parents’ rights in schools.

Here’s where LGBTQ+ rights are on the ballot this November.

Arizona voters will decide this fall whether trans student-athletes may continue to compete on school sports teams that align with their gender identity. A ballot initiative introduced late last year by state Rep. Selina Bliss, a Republican running for reelection, would effectively restore a 2022 state law restricting trans athletes’ participation that a federal appeals court had blocked in 2024.

Kris Mayes, Arizona’s Democratic attorney general, has declined to defend the law in court.

Bliss’ proposal would require public and qualifying private schools to designate K-12 sports teams as exclusively “male,” “female” or “coeducational” based on participating students’ “biological status at birth.” It would also bar trans students from using restrooms, locker rooms and other spaces “integral to athletic engagement” that match their gender identity.

In July, a lawsuit challenging the measure claimed it violated a requirement that Arizona ballot initiatives address only a single subject and was “misleading to the point of fraud.” A state superior court judge later ruled that the initiative could remain on the November 3 ballot.

Colorado voters will decide whether to bar trans student-athletes from competing in line with their gender identity by designating K-12 and collegiate sports teams based on students’ “biological reproductive systems.” The ballot initiative qualified for the general election after Protect Kids Colorado, the organization behind it, collected more than 168,000 signatures statewide.

Voters will also decide whether to ban transition-related surgeries for minors, and whether state or federal funds, Medicaid reimbursements or insurance coverage can be used to help pay for them. Such surgeries are already rare. The measure, also introduced by Protect Kids Colorado, does not directly mention nonsurgical care.

State medical organizations, including the Colorado Academy of Family Physicians and the Colorado Medical Society (CMS), the state’s largest organized group of practitioners, have publicly opposed the healthcare-related initiative. “CMS members hold diverse political views but share a core principle: medical decisions belong in the exam room,” Brigitta Robinson, the organization’s president, said in September.

That initiative also runs counter to “shield laws” safeguarding access to gender-affirming healthcare, as well as abortion, in Colorado.

In Missouri, voters will decide whether to reverse a 2024 amendment adding abortion protections to the state constitution. The new proposal would ban abortions in almost all cases, with exceptions for rape and incest, though only through the first trimester, and in medical emergencies throughout pregnancy.

It would also add language to the state constitution banning gender-affirming medical care for trans minors — prohibited by law in Missouri since 2023. An ultimately unsuccessful effort to disqualify the proposal from the November ballot, led by the ACLU of Missouri, claimed the measure violated the state’s single subject clause for ballot initiatives and failed to adequately inform voters of its intent.

Voters in Nebraska will decide whether to add language to the state constitution requiring public and qualifying private schools to designate athletic teams based on “biological sex,” and expressly declare that girls’ sports “shall not be open to students of the male sex.”

The ballot initiative qualified for the general election in August, after organizers collected more than 130,000 signatures from across the state. The following month, Nebraska voter Cara Ulman filed a lawsuit to disqualify the measure. Her legal team argued before the state Supreme Court in September that the measure’s sponsors had failed to “adequately inform the public of what they are trying to accomplish” with the initiative.

Because Nebraska’s secretary of state has already certified its general election ballot, the measure will go before voters regardless of the court’s decision, which is expected by October 27. But a ruling in Ulman’s favor would invalidate the results.

Nebraska law already prohibits trans student-athletes from participating in sports in line with their gender identity from kindergarten through college.

Voters in Vermont will decide this fall whether to add an equal rights amendment to the state constitution. The proposal, introduced in 2023 by a coalition of Democratic state lawmakers, would prohibit unequal treatment “on account of a person’s race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin.” In Vermont, a constitutional amendment must pass two legislative sessions before it can go before voters.

Virginia voters will decide whether to repeal language in the state constitution barring same-sex couples from marrying, and instead establish an affirmative right to marriage between two consenting adults regardless of their sex, gender or race. The proposal, first introduced in 2024, qualified for the November ballot after several failed attempts. In Virginia, proposed amendments to the constitution must be approved by the state House and Senate twice before they can appear before voters.

Virginia’s ban on gay marriage, added to its constitution in 2006, has been unenforceable since 2015, when the Supreme Court established a federal right to marry for same-sex couples in the United States. But marriage equality advocates have argued that recent decisions and public statements by the high court’s conservative supermajority have put that right in jeopardy. The Supreme Court declined to take up a case challenging its same-sex marriage ruling last fall.

Voters in Washington will decide whether to bar trans student-athletes from girls’ school sports teams by requiring every girl in the state to have her sex assigned at birth verified by a doctor — through either genetic or hormone tests or an examination of her reproductive anatomy — to determine eligibility for K-12 sports.

Opponents of the initiative have said it can be easily exploited, putting both trans and cisgender girls at risk of abuse. In a July op-ed, women’s soccer superstar Megan Rapinoe, a Washington native, argued the measure would drive some girls out of sports altogether.

The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has allowed trans students to compete in line with their gender identity since 2007.

The initiative qualified for the November ballot in January, after Let’s Go Washington, the political action committee behind it, collected more than 440,000 petition signatures from across the state. The group, founded by conservative hedge fund manager Brian Heywood, is also behind a second ballot measure to restore a 2024 state law regarding students’ and parents’ rights in public schools.

Washington’s Democratic-controlled legislature amended the law, known as the parental “bill of rights,” last spring, saying it was necessary to comply with existing state and federal laws. The new proposal would effectively reverse the 2025 changes.

State LGBTQ+ organizations and Democratic politicians — including Gov. Bob Ferguson — have opposed the initiative, arguing that it would put LGBTQ+ students at risk of being outed to unsupportive parents, among other safety and privacy concerns.
