author: Jen Fifield
title: Ballot Rejections Soared in Rural Counties After USPS Cost-Cutting Measures
content:
The rates of primary ballots rejected for arriving late this year doubled or tripled in some areas compared to 2022.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.

Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.

Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.

In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail.

But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.

Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.

The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.

In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.

In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.

Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.

Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.

“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”

Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.

At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.

“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”

Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.

“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.’”

A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)

After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.

At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.

Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.

“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”

Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.

The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots, even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006.

When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration. (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)

The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since.

Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.

The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.

In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.

This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.

Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.

A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.

“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,’” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”

Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.

Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.

In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.

In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.

In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.

“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”

In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.

Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.

Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.

Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.

Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.

The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.

ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.)

Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.

“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher.

Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.

A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.

In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.

Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen.

In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.

“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.

author: Sara Luterman
title: Nursing Home Residents Have a Right to Vote — Despite What Trump CMS Agency Says
content:
The Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Cindy Napolitan and her daughter Melissa have multiple sclerosis, a degenerative condition in which the immune system attacks the brain, spinal cord and nerves. They have lived together at a nursing home in Mesquite, Texas, for nine years. In previous elections, Cindy and Melissa Napolitan voted by mail, but this year they took an unusual step: They voted in person. They worried their mail-in ballots — and even their in-person votes — may not be counted.

“I’ve never worried like this before. I’ve never worried that I don’t have the proper ID. I’ve never worried that somebody is going to intimidate me. Will I encounter somebody that’s going to threaten me or make me feel less than? So yeah, I’m very worried, and I shouldn’t be,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I shouldn’t have to be worried about stuff like that. This is the 19th Amendment. I’m allowed to vote.”

Nursing home residents are guaranteed the right to vote. Around two-thirds of all nursing home residents in the United States are women, making aging and long-term care gendered issues.

There is no data on how many nursing home residents exercise that right. Cindy, 70, and Melissa Napolitan, 48, at least, feel like they’ve had good experiences with voting at their facility. Cindy Napolitan, in particular, has worked with the activities coordinator to organize rides to the polls for her, her daughter and other interested residents.

“We are scheduled to go on the first day of early voting. So in case there are any issues that we come across, we still have time to rectify the situation and be allowed to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan are more concerned this year than in previous years about government interference and voter suppression. Their fears are not unfounded: Experts and advocates for the rights of nursing home residents, older adults and people with disabilities are worried too.

In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rescinded previous guidance affirming that nursing home residents have the right to vote.

“The memo does not alter the underlying law. Nursing homes are governed by the Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 and its implementing regulations,” said Nina Kohn, a professor at Syracuse University and expert on elder law. “That law still requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights as Americans.”

The memo also emphasized voter fraud in nursing homes, specifically around mail-in ballots. For years, President Trump has disparaged mail-in ballots, insisting without evidence that fraudulent votes by mail had a role in his loss during the 2020 presidential election. His comments have led to some states restricting who can use a mail-in ballot and in what contexts.

According to experts, including Kohn, there is no evidence that voter fraud is a serious or widespread problem in nursing homes. Instead, Kohn is concerned about the chilling effect that it may have on residents’ rights.

“The language in the memo itself is intimidating, and it may understandably make staff think that they could face criminal prosecution or be in some other form of legal trouble if they help residents vote,” Kohn said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan do everything together — and on Monday, they voted together. They are also roommates at the facility; most people living in nursing homes are assigned roommates who are strangers.

“Unlike other people that have roommates that don’t get along, I’m very lucky and fortunate that I have somebody that loves me and I love her,” Cindy Napolitan said.

This is the second time Cindy and Melissa Napolitan have voted in person since entering a nursing home. The first time was during the 2024 presidential election.

“I’ve been checking my status weekly to make sure that I haven’t been dropped off the voter rolls, making sure my daughter and I don’t have some sort of issue that says that we can’t vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

People living in nursing homes and other long-term care facilities face specific barriers. Some residents may need assistance filling out their ballots because they lack the movement or dexterity to hold a pen or press buttons on a computer screen. People with dexterity or coordination issues may also be unable to produce the same signature twice.

“With some forms of voting, some states will use your ID to verify your signature. If your signature looks different than the one on your ID, your ballot might get thrown out. Or there is a ballot hearing process, so you could be notified of that and able to fix it, but it is a bunch of extra steps that impact disabled voters at higher rates,” said Alexia Kemerling, director of Accessible Democracy for the nonpartisan American Association of People with Disabilities.

An increasing number of states now require voters to show some form of photo identification. This can also be a problem for many nursing home residents because they may no longer have a driver’s license. They also may no longer have passports because they aren’t traveling internationally. States have other forms of identification, but getting them can involve complex paperwork and multiple trips.

Some states will accommodate voters in nursing homes and other facilities so they can acquire state identification that isn’t a driver’s license.

“My license expired, and so I had to apply for an identification card. I had to coordinate with them to come here instead of going to the DMV because I wasn’t about to do that. I didn’t know how long I would have to sit there. I didn’t have a ride,” Melissa Napolitan said. “They came and took our pictures, and filled out all the forms for us.”

Kemerling objects to the idea that this somehow renders nursing home residents and other people with disabilities incapable of making an independent choice.

“In the disability community, we don’t necessarily mean that independence means doing something alone. Independence is having control over how something is done,” Kemerling said. “Just because you need someone to assist you as part of the voting process does not mean that you are giving up your choice.”

There are steps nursing home residents and their families can take to advocate for their rights. Lori Smetanka is the executive director of the National Consumer Voice for Quality Long Term Care, which advocates on behalf of people living in nursing homes and assisted living facilities. Her organization produces a fact sheet for nursing home residents enumerating their rights and how they can advocate for themselves.

“For the generation of people that are living in long-term care facilities, it’s largely an older population of people,” Smetanka said. “It’s very important to them to exercise their right to vote. When we talk with residents, it is very important to them. Some of them have really advocated very heavily for themselves in order to be able to do that.”

Smetanka emphasized that it is not only up to residents and their families to advocate for their rights.

“If the resident has the ability to raise the questions about it, they certainly should be doing that, Smetanka said. “Families should be asking, but staff should be asking too — ‘What can we do to help you vote this year? Who is interested in voting? How can we get the requirements in place so you can cast your ballots?’” At some facilities, voting may not be on staff’s radar, despite the legal requirements.

Cindy Napolitan has been active in advocating for her right to vote, as well as the rights of her fellow residents, and she encourages others who are able to do the same.

“I’m very vocal and very into advocating for our residents here and making sure that they’re all able to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I’m the one that will start telling our activity director that there’s a deadline for filing to become a registered voter. There’s a deadline to file for a mail-in ballot, and I’m usually the one that makes sure that those things get done.”

When asked what she wants people to understand most about voting in nursing homes, Melissa Napolitan pushed back against the insinuation that nursing homes are hotbeds of voter fraud and that she and her peers don’t have their own opinions.

“I think that people maybe don’t take the time to realize that people in nursing homes aren’t just here waiting to die,” Melissa Napolitan said.

author: Jon Letman
title: Trump’s Anti-DEI Agenda Threatens to Slash Land Mine Disposal Efforts Globally
content:
The Trump administration’s expansion of its global gag rule threatens to derail NGOs’ crucial land mine removal work.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

US funding for overseas nongovernment organizations (NGOs) is now at risk. Due to a global gag rule that the Trump administration introduced early in 2026, government funding for certain foreign aid programs is subject to more stringent restrictions on activities related to diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI); abortion access; and what the Trump administration calls “gender ideology” (which includes gender-affirming counseling and care, as well as basic inclusion of and respect for transgender people). These restrictions are all occurring under what the State Department calls the Promoting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance policy.

Norwegian People’s Aid (NPA), a leading NGO doing land mine removal and disarmament work around the world, announced it will decline U.S. funding due to these new restrictions. In a press release, NPA Secretary General Raymond Johansen said the new requirements run contrary to the organization’s commitment to its core values including gender equality and diversity; therefore, it was forced to forego critical U.S. government support.

“We comply with Norwegian law and Norwegian policy, and our values are not for sale,” Johansen said.

The loss of financial support will have a major impact on NPA’s work removing anti-personnel land mines, cluster munitions, and unexploded ordnance left over from past wars and conflicts. The loss of 400 million Norwegian kroners (NOK) — around $42 million in U.S. dollars — in support from the State Department represents around 40 percent of NPA’s budget for clearing mines and bombs in 20 countries.

Overseas funding restrictions have existed under past presidents going back to the Reagan administration in 1984, but with the expansion of the gag rule, new requirements won’t only affect funding for U.S. programs, but will impact all NPA programs, Gry Ballestad, NPA’s director of policy and communications, told Truthout in an interview. “It will affect everything we do globally and this is what makes it different,” Ballestad said. NPA expects the loss of funding to result in 1,700 job cuts globally, including over 1,000 staff in Laos.

Although U.S. government funding for NPA is limited to mine removal programs, the new requirements could impact its global work, which includes international development programs and working with women’s organizations that may support abortion rights, LGBTQ rights, and anti-racism activities in Norway and elsewhere. NPA programs include refugee and integration, support for humanitarian aid, and addressing gender wealth disparities.

The loss in support from the State Department represents around 40 percent of NPA’s budget for clearing mines and bombs in 20 countries.

The loss of U.S. funding will have a major impact not only on NPA mine programs, but on the entire organization, Ballestad said, adding that while most donors impose conditions, the new restrictions run contrary to past requirements and may contradict those of other donors. She called the imposition of these funding requirements a political decision which has the potential to wield control over 400 million NOK for mine removal programs — and which could place NPA’s total budget of more than 1.6 billion NOK in legal jeopardy.

Ballestad said this represents a greater challenge to norms and regulations going back many decades: “We’ve never seen this before from a donor putting requirements that will affect the rest of your funding.”

Speaking Out for Democracy and Freedom

After months of legal consultations with lawyers in the U.S. and an unsuccessful attempt to receive a waiver for Southeast Asia where it does the majority of its mine work, NPA determined it had no choice but to uphold its principles, values, and obligations to its membership. “We can’t just change that because there’s a new American administration that comes up with new regulations … We’re a democratic organization,” Ballestad said. NPA’s outspoken position has received widespread support from labor unions and the Norwegian public.

NPA surveyed more than 5.3 million square meters for cluster munition contamination in 2025. Now that work will end.

Jon Jensen, NPA’s section leader of the Middle East and Central Asia, told Truthout in an interview that the loss of State Department funding will mean a significant reduction of field operations like clearing areas contaminated by cluster munitions and explosive ordnance. This includes working with other mine action operators and Laotian government authorities mapping and identifying hazardous areas based on data and consultations with local communities.

According to a Mine Action Review Report, NPA surveyed more than 5.3 million square meters for cluster munition contamination in 2025. Now that work will end.

“As of now, we have stopped all field operations in Laos and sent out termination notices to around a thousand staff,” Jensen said.

Although the loss of U.S. government funding will force the closure of some programs or reduce mine-clearing activities, Ballestad said 60 percent of NPA’s mine action work will continue as it searches for alternate funding sources. Hardest hit will be Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, and the Pacific nation of Palau.

Where possible, NPA plans to hand over staff, materials, and equipment to other organizations, but the process isn’t easy, and not all organizations do the same kind of work. Jensen added that although NPA was unable to accept funding under the new conditions, it was still cooperating with the State Department’s Office of Weapons Removal and Abatement to coordinate a smooth handover to different operators who could take on some of NPA’s work, trying to minimize the negative impacts for communities polluted by explosive remnants of war.

Hardest hit will be Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, and the Pacific nation of Palau.

The State Department did not provide a response to multiple requests from Truthout seeking comment for this story.

NPA is not alone in rejecting U.S. funding under the new requirements: Organizations like Save the Children Norway also face foreign aid cuts while Norwegian Church Aid took a similar position to NPA in declining funding under the new Trump administration conditions. In a statement, its secretary general, Anne Cecilie Kaltenborn, said, “humanitarian principles are not for sale.”

NPA began international humanitarian mine removal efforts in Cambodia in 1992 and has received U.S. funding since the mid-1990s. Since that time, NPA says it has cleared more than 2 million land mines and explosives in 45 countries from Iraq, Yemen, and Ukraine to Angola and Peru.

Buried munitions which did not detonate continue to maim and kill civilians, more than half of them children.

The group’s mine work currently includes 20 countries with major field operations in Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam. According to NPA, in the 1960s and ’70s, the United States dropped more than 400,000 tons of cluster bombs on Vietnam, while neighboring Cambodia and Laos are among the most heavily mined and bombed countries in the world. According to an estimate from the government of Laos, the U.S. military dropped more than 270 million submunitions over nine years of secret warfare (1964-1973).

Today, buried munitions which did not detonate continue to maim and kill civilians, more than half of them children, frequently while in villages and rice fields. Some 12,000 unexploded ordnance accidents have been documented in Laos since 1973, according to government of Laos data.

“Most of the contamination that we are addressing with U.S. funding also has a U.S. origin.”

Decades after wars in Southeast Asia ended, the remnants of war continue to hinder economic development and pose significant risks to civilians, a danger which increases as aging weapons grow more unstable over time, said Jensen, adding, “most of the contamination that we are addressing with U.S. funding also has a U.S. origin.”

The use of land mines in Southeast Asia is not limited to long-ago wars. As recently as 2025, mines were allegedly used on the border between Cambodia and Thailand, sparking deadly clashes.

Despite the need to continue mine-clearing work, NPA insists it will not betray its own values and those of members and supporters. “If somebody gives us money, it is because they support our work and the values that we stand for,” Ballestad says. “However, if private donors in any country give us money, they will be under the regulations of a U.S. administration that may be contradicting what those donors want to support. I think people understand that and they don’t think it’s right.”

title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid to Halt Care for Incarcerated Trans People
content:
The decision is a rare win for transgender rights at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The U.S. Supreme Court has denied an emergency petition from the Trump administration, which sought a stay on a lower court’s injunction on a policy that would have denied gender-affirming care to federally incarcerated transgender people.

That policy was implemented by the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 that denied the existence of transgender people. The order also directed federal agencies to take steps that would be consistent with that view, and included specific instructions for the BOP.

“The Attorney General shall ensure that the Bureau of Prisons revises its policies concerning medical care to be consistent with this order, and shall ensure that no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex,” the order reads.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Albania Protests Escalate Over Corruption, Planned Kushner/Trump Luxury Resort
content:
Student-led anti-corruption and cost-of-living protests call for the prime minister’s resignation, among other demands.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Student-led anti-corruption and cost-of-living protests in Albania are calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, among other demands. Hundreds of injuries and arrests have been reported amid a violent police crackdown, along with widespread damage to public and private property. The student demands are an outgrowth of the “Flamingo Revolution,” which erupted earlier this year in opposition to a luxury resort being developed on the ecologically sensitive Sazan Island. The planned resort is backed by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, President Trump’s son-in-law and daughter, and has been fast-tracked by the Rama government.

“Students find no future in Albania,” says Bora Mema, a founding member of the left-wing political party Lëvizja Bashkë, about the motivations behind the burgeoning pro-democracy movement. “Many of us have to migrate because the only development model that the government proposes is to clean the toilets of the rich and the mafia in luxurious resorts, like the one that Trump and Kushner and the national oligarchs and mafia in Albania are constructing.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: In Albania, student-led anti-government protests have rocked the capital Tirana for more than a week, as thousands have taken to the streets to call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Last week, the Albanian Student Union called for strikes and demonstrations at the Ministry of Education to protest high tuition costs, poor university conditions, a lack of jobs, and corruption. At least half a million young Albanians have left the country over the last decade in search of better economic opportunities.

Initial protests have escalated into ongoing clashes with police, leading to hundreds of injuries and arrests, widespread damage to government buildings, street lights and private property. Riot police have deployed tear gas, water cannons, sound grenades and rubber bullets against the protesters. These are some of those protesters in their own words.

LULJETA KOLA: [translated] What does Albania want? It wants a revolution, a change, a complete overthrow of the system, because it can’t go on like this, because these people have become billionaires, superbillionaires, and there are very poor people here.

ULIKS SKENDERAJ: The economy, like education, healthcare, everything, has gone downhill since many years. Yeah, basically. But all of the — all of the politicians from both parties, the main parties, should be gone, basically. This is what the new generation wants.

NDERIME VLADI: For us to stop the protests, first of all, Edi Rama should resign, immediately. Like, at the second that he resigns, his whole Cabinet should resign. … They deserve prison for every corruption that they have done. They have done so many. I mean, I cannot begin to, like, count with my fingers what they have done with this country. The corruption is on levels unseen, unseen in any other state of the world.

ANJALI KAMAT: Albania’s protests first began in May, when environmentalists rallied against a luxury resort development on the ecologically sensitive Sazan Island. The project is backed by President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and has been fast-tracked by the Albanian government. Protests against the development grew into what is known as the Flamingo movement, which has rallied against government corruption for months and has now been joined by students in this latest wave of unrest.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Edi Rama set up chairs outside Parliament in a symbolic gesture for dialogue. Protesters calling for his resignation later smashed the chairs. Rama is leader of the Socialist Party and has a majority in Parliament. He’s been in power for 13 years and has so far refused to resign. The next elections are scheduled for 2029. During a live stream on Sunday, Rama said protests could hurt Albania’s bid to join the European Union by 2030, and claimed protesters were linked to antifa.

PRIME MINISTER EDI RAMA: [translated] They are young men and women who have ideologized and radicalized under pressure or inspiration of the dark and new force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, which the president of the United States has designated a terrorist organization: antifa.

AMY GOODMAN: For more, we’re joined by Bora Mema, longtime labor organizer, researcher and activist. She’s also a founding member of the left-wing political party Lëvizja Bashkë, which means “movement together.” We spoke to her from Albania in July. Today, she’s joining us from London.

Bora, thanks so much for joining us again. If you can describe what is happening in the streets today in Tirana and around Albania, the dramatic scenes that are unfolding in the streets, and also how it all began, this development on Sazan Island, backed by President Trump’s son-in-law and his daughter, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump?

BORA MEMA: Thank you, Amy, for having me again in Democracy Now! It’s a very — it’s an honor for me and also for everyone who has been protesting for months to be in this program again and to represent and to speak up about what’s happening in Albania.

The last week has been quite dramatic due to the fact that the violence and the brutalism that the police have been showing to the protesters has never been seen in the country before, not even in 1991, when the Communist Party of Albania was still in power and it was a one-state party and it was a dictatorial regime. So, what we have been seeing so far is something unseen in the streets of Albania.

This is — this is not a separate protest. It’s not just a student protest. This is part of the ongoing more than 143 days of the Flamingo Revolution on the streets. But it has a huge turn, because after more than 135 days of peaceful protests — although there were many arrests and brutality shown by the police in specific protests close to the Parliament as they happen each week, all the other days have been quite peaceful protests.

What we’ve seen since last week, since last Tuesday, is that, since, the students decided to boycott the university. So, the academic year starts in Albania in the beginning of October, and students decided that there is no point to go to university for as long as there is this huge protest happening for so many months. There is massive corruption since the start of the protests with opposing the Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump hijacking the Sazan Island and the natural protected areas of Zvërnec in southwest of Albanian coastline. Students decided to boycott the classes. Professors are supporting students.

And it’s this outrage, because so many other corruption scandals have been identified during summer, so many other ministers or high functionaries, like the head of the Albanian secret service, like the Albanian CIA. She’s under house arrest because she was found out to be having an affair and also to leak state secret data to the underground prime minister of Albania, Ergys Agasi, which is the guy who does all the dirty work for Edi Rama.

So, all this outrage and the fact that students find no future in Albania. You must have seen — you also mentioned it before, that hundred thousands of people have left the country in one decade. Most of them are young people, people who see no future, people who are forced to be migrants, just like myself. We don’t want to be migrants. We want to live in our country, but we are forced to leave the country because there are no jobs. There is no — there is no future for us. It’s impossible for Albanians to even pay the rent or to have the prices higher than in so many supermarkets, even compared to Germany. The prices in supermarkets are higher than in Germany. But when it comes to the wages, they are the lowest in Europe, or the pensions. Like, many of us have to migrate because we need to support our retired parents. Many of us have to migrate because the only development model that the government proposes is to clean the toilets of the rich and the mafia in luxurious resorts, like the one that Trump and Kushner and the national oligarchs and mafia in Albania are constructing.

So, it started as environmental and against the land grab and protest, and it has developed into huge anti-corruption protests, that even if you compare it to the other protests happening around Europe, mostly from students and the youth, it has more an anti-systematic protest. As you heard, people demand a revolution. They want democracy. They want democracy now. Albania is living in an authoritarian regime.

Unfortunately, as you mentioned, the police violence has been extreme. There are more than 500 people being arrested, and due to the fact that the police stations are full, the police is now beating up the people severely, even peaceful protesters or people who are even randomly walking on the streets, beating up to break their limbs so they can’t go out on the protests in the following — in the following days. People who have been kept in prison cells — although the court has stated that these are illegal arrests, they’ve been kept there for many days. And in the first 72 hours, they have even been deprived from water and food.

So, we have an extreme breach and violation of human rights, and it’s terrifying if you think about the fact that Albania is a country that is supposed to join EU before 2030. And unfortunately, you see the European commissioner or the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, who say that they trust that the government will fulfill their promise and meet their criterias to join EU.

ANJALI KAMAT: And, Bora, can you explain who the prime minister is, Edi Rama? He’s from the center-left Socialist Party. But the kind of repression that we’re seeing on the streets and the bravery of the protesters, where does this discontent come from?

BORA MEMA: Edi Rama pretends he is center-left, but he changes his position depending on what his interests are. So, he can pretend he’s a socialist. He can have an anti-fascist rhetoric when it comes to a specific socialist electorate who is nostalgic of — due to the anti-fascist legacy of Second World War. And he is not worried at all to kneel to Giorgia Meloni, the far-right prime minister of Italy, to sit or also to have negotiations and have refugee camps in Albania as an extraterritorial, which is against international law, because refugees are being sent from Italy into camps, like, to prisons in Albania. So, when it comes to his own interests, Edi Rama doesn’t care.

Edi Rama says he’s the head of the Socialist Party, and he is the head of the Socialist Party, but Socialist Party is not even center-left. It’s not even right. It’s a criminal organization. It’s an organized crime organization linked to the mafia. There are so many international reports that state that Albania is a narco-state. Albania is controlled by the mafia. Even the latest arrests and prosecutions that have been sent forward by the special prosecutor, supported by the EU, because it’s independent — luckily, it’s not dependent on the Albanian government — most of the cases are people linked to the mafia. Many scandals, many investigations, even from the Italian or international prosecutor offices that show the links between ministers and the mafia and the international mafia. So, the Socialist Party, it’s not a matter of ideological question, if it’s — is it a social democratic, or is it democratic left, or is it socialist, or is it neoliberal, as all the neoliberal policies that have been implementing so far, but it’s a matter of: Are they an organized organization, or are they a political party?

On the other hand, Edi Rama is not ashamed to say that in Albania there are no trade unions, so he invites foreign investors to come to Albania because there are no trade unions. Edi Rama pretends he’s socialist, but he has implemented the most austerity, repressive policies, than even compared to his other — to the former prime ministers, who have been also very authoritarian and right-wing prime ministers. Edi Rama pretends he’s a socialist, but he is not ashamed to use — to pretend that these protests are supported by antifa. First of all, even this is not true. This is [bleep]. It’s just his way to appeal to Trump, just in the same way as he is appealing to Trump by selling — not even by selling, by giving away our land.

I need to — I am also very sorry to the state that the American — the United States diplomacy has ended up that even a corrupt prime minister of a small country like Albania has the ability to bribe the president or the son-in-law of the president of the United States, although — so, of course, like, this — I’m so sorry for speaking like this, but, unfortunately, this is the state of the American diplomacy, and it shows that Rama is using antifa as a way to appeal even more to President Trump. This is [bleep], and this is [bleep]. There is no link between antifa in Europe or U.S. linked to what is happening in Albania.

But let’s assume for a moment that this is antifa. “Antifa” stands for “anti-fascist.” And of course that our protests are anti-fascist. We are not — the only fascist — the only only fascist thing happening is the repression from the police and from the government, which is threatening teachers that they are going to be dismissed for supporting students, which is threatening parents that they are not going to see their kids. It’s putting pressure on journalists, who have been — some of them have even been hit with rubber bullets, and journalists being dismissed and pressured if they speak up the truth and they are in the protests. This is fascism. Anti-anti-fascism is actually fascism. And unfortunately, this is what is happening right now.

AMY GOODMAN: Bora Mema, Bora, we want to thank you so much.

AMY GOODMAN: We want to thank you so much for being with us, Bora Mema, longtime labor organizer, researcher and activist, also founding member of the left political party Lëvizja Bashkë.

Coming up, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, co-authors of the new book End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World. Stay with us.

title: FCC Chair Brendan Carr Threatens Broadcasters Over Poll Coverage
content:
A Democratic strategist points out that “it’s not illegal to tell the American people that Trump is a failed president.”

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr on Wednesday threatened broadcasters that cover what he described as “fake polls,” which he said hurt “voter turnout and enthusiasm.”

In a social media post, Carr attacked news outlets for “amplifying or airing these polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis.”

Carr did not provide a single specific example of a “fake” opinion poll, nor did he name a broadcaster who has promoted one. President Donald Trump, who nominated Carr to head the FCC, has repeatedly decried polls as “fake” as they’ve shown his approval ratings at record lows.

Later in the post, Carr hinted that the FCC would take direct action against broadcasters for informing their viewers about opinion polls.

“The FCC takes these issues seriously,” said Carr. “Broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in news distortion or promoting broadcast hoaxes. It is important that broadcasters comply with their public interest obligations.”

title: Dispatch From Paris: Student-Led Protests Spread, Despite Brutal Policing
content:

author: Chris Walker
title: Acton Says Ramaswamy Exploited Her Estranged Mother for Political Gain
content:
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton accused her mother’s then-husband of sexual assault when she was a child.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Democratic candidate for Ohio governor Amy Acton has responded to a political ad produced by her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign, which features her mother — whom she’s been estranged from for decades — describing Acton as a liar.

The ad is being widely criticized as distasteful because Acton accused her mother and her then-stepfather of abuse and sexual assault when she was just a child.

In the ad, Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, is shown speaking directly into the camera about her daughter, whom she has not seen since 1978, when Acton was just 12 years old.

“Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar,” Arthur says. “She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help.”

The ad doesn’t mention why Arthur believes her daughter is a liar, and it leaves out all relevant information about their estrangement.

Acton alleges that she was the victim of sexual abuse by Arthur’s now-deceased husband when she was between the ages of 10 and 12. Acton has also recalled being unhoused at one point while living with her mother and stepfather.

She later told her father about the abuses, and a grand jury indicted her stepfather. Her mother and stepfather then fled the state to avoid prosecution, Acton has recounted.

The ad did not indicate who paid for or produced it. Though the Ramaswamy campaign had initially avoided taking responsibility for the ad, it has now admitted they made the commercial. What’s more, the campaign intends to spend an additional $4 million to continue airing it.

The campaign defended the ad in a statement.

“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor,” the Ramaswamy campaign said.

On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance came to Ramaswamy’s defense.

“Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” Vance said in response to a reporter’s question, saying he was more focused on the election’s outcome.

“Have the opinion you want to have on that ad,” Vance continued, adding that he was “disgusted” at members of his own party “whining” about the contents of the ad.

Acton has condemned Ramaswamy for the ad in a statement posted on Facebook.

“Between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me. … I’ve always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it’s sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain,” Acton said.

I know what it feels like to be a child who is hungry, frightened, and uncertain of what tomorrow will bring. I know what it means to feel powerless and to depend on the courage and compassion of others to find a way forward. Those experiences shaped my values, my compassion, and my belief that every person deserves to be safe, to be heard, and to have a fair chance at a better life. They are part of what led me to become a doctor, to dedicate my life to public service, and to fight for people who too often feel forgotten or left behind.

Acton’s brother, Phillip Stearns, has also blasted the ad.

“It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” Stearns said in a statement, adding that the commercial is a “desperate, disgusting attack” that “reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”

The race between Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, and Ramaswamy, an ally of President Donald Trump, is a tight one. According to an average of polling data compiled by FiftyPlusOne, Acton is currently leading the contest, garnering around 49 percent of support in the state, while Ramaswamy receives 44.5 percent.

title: Nurses Just Helped Win US’s First Countywide 12-Week Paid Parental Leave Policy
content:

As a nurse in the neonatal intensive care unit, Jean Stone knows what it really means to live in a country with no paid parental leave.

She’s watched this scene play out so many times it’s almost the norm: Once their babies stabilize in the NICU, parents often return to work to preserve whatever parental leave they have left for when their babies come home. Stone calls the parents in the middle of the day to update them — starting each call with, “Everything is OK” — and watch them come in at the end of their workday, their faces reflecting the relief of reunion.

“They carry that weight of not being there,” Stone, who works at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital in Pittsburgh, told The 19th.

Five months ago, she and the other nurses at Magee, who are in the middle of negotiating a union contract, decided to do something about it. They came together with a coalition of working parents, advocates and some elected leaders to draft a proposal for a paid leave program in Allegheny County. author: Blanca Missé
title: As More Unions Oppose ICE and Israel, the Right Is Cracking Down
content:
The right is trying to gain access to labor unions’ minutes, membership lists, and Zoom chats.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On September 22, The Free Press attacked the California Faculty Association (CFA), which represents about 29,000 faculty, librarians, counselors, and coaches across the California State University (CSU) system. Drawing on private discussions about a proposed Jewish caucus, including communications from a union Zoom meeting, the article accused CFA of antisemitism. How those communications reached the publication remains unclear. Two days later, the Jewish Journal amplified those allegations, urging Gov. Gavin Newsom to consider them as he weighed California Assembly Bill (AB) 2551, CFA-sponsored legislation challenging campus protest restrictions imposed after the 2024 Palestine solidarity encampments. Less than a week after The Free Press story was published, Newsom vetoed the bill.

Pro-Israel and Jewish advocacy organizations had already campaigned against AB 2551 before the union’s internal deliberations were targeted, arguing that greater scrutiny would weaken rules needed to protect Jewish students from harassment and intimidation. Newsom’s veto does not prove coordination, but the campaign portraying CFA as hostile to Jewish students had become entangled with the union’s fight against campus protest restrictions.

The CSU’s systemwide policy prohibits encampments, overnight demonstrations, and unauthorized structures. The CSU Academic Senate immediately condemned the restrictions as undermining academic freedom when it was instituted in 2024, while CFA warned that vague definitions of disruption threatened constitutionally protected speech, assembly, protest, and future strike activity. A major 2026 ACLU-Amnesty study, investigating 80 campuses over two years, documented sweeping repression of Palestine solidarity protests. As the report found, universities “have imposed sweeping restrictions on student speech, initiated disciplinary actions against students, and imposed severe punishments, including expulsions and suspensions.” The ACLU has insisted that even legitimate time, place, and manner restrictions “must leave ample room for students to express themselves.”

The controversy reaches beyond CFA and CSU. Unions and rank-and-file organizations committed to Palestine solidarity have been forced to relitigate, again and again, whether anti-Zionism and solidarity with Palestinians constitute antisemitism — and whether such organizing should be systematically policed, investigated, or surveilled. At stake is a more fundamental right of the exploited: Can workers democratically connect economic struggles with Palestine solidarity, resistance to anti-immigrant and anti-Black racism, and the defense of civil liberties without exposing their organizing and deliberations to external pressure or repression?

We already have a word for the use of legal process as a political weapon: lawfare. You do not necessarily have to win. Investigation, expense, compelled disclosure, and possible sanctions can exact their own price.

Call its media counterpart pressfare: leaked material, selective or doctored quotations, and public identification can turn people into political targets and invite pressure on employers, universities, or government agencies.

The leaked CFA meeting should not be adjudicated through fragments selected for publication, especially when CFA’s statewide record contradicts the portrayal of a union indifferent to antisemitism. During the 2024 encampments, CFA opposed antisemitism and Islamophobia “in all forms” while supporting the encampments. Amid a 2025 federal antisemitism investigation, it stated that “as CFA members, we are united against antisemitism; it has no place in our communities,” while defending members’ academic freedom. CFA’s Palestine, Arab, and Muslim Caucus likewise defines its mission as confronting racism “in all its manifestations,” explicitly including antisemitism. The Free Press story — a clear example of pressfare — sought to overwrite this legacy with weaponized accusations, undermining the trust that workers place in the sanctity of their union spaces and processes.

Antisemitism demands to be taken seriously — which is why accusations of anti-Jewish discrimination should not be instrumentalized. Kenneth Stern, director of the Bard Center for the Study of Hate, has warned that using the International Holocaust Remembrance Association (IHRA) definition of antisemitism as a regulatory code threatens academic freedom by equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, while the Jerusalem Declaration warns that the definition’s ambiguities have generated confusion and controversy, “hence weakening the fight against antisemitism.” And as Jewish Voice for Peace and Jerusalem Declaration scholars have argued, combating antisemitism is not helped by conflating hostility toward Jews with anti-Zionism, criticism of Israel, or Palestine solidarity. Requiring Palestinian and anti-Zionist unionists to prove otherwise reverses the burden of proof, allowing accusations to substitute for evidence and cultivating fear and suspicion that inhibit collective action while fueling an ever-expanding search for evidence.

That ever-expanding search has taken the form of several federal antisemitism inquiries targeting universities and their workers.

Federal antisemitism investigations have extended scrutiny to faculty speech and Palestine solidarity organizing, with consequences for unions. At Cal State LA, CSU disclosed employees’ personal information to federal investigators, prompting CFA to sue over violations of workers’ privacy.

What drove these federal inquiries on antisemitism? A 2025 study from the American Association of University Professors and the Middle East Studies Association examined 102 complaints that prompted federal civil rights investigations; pro-Israel and right-wing organizations were involved in 78 percent. All but one of the complaints concerned speech critical of Israel, and in 80 percent, complainants characterized criticism of Israel or Zionism that made no reference to Jews or Judaism as antisemitic. In at least half, the complaint rested solely on constitutionally protected political speech.

The study separately examined 28 Title VI antisemitism lawsuits brought against universities by pro-Israel groups. As of its cutoff, not one had produced a final judicial finding of discrimination in favor of the plaintiffs, although some resulted in settlements imposing new restrictions on campus speech and protest.

CFA’s political commitments long predate the renewed Palestine solidarity movement. In 2023, the union challenged CSU administrators on First Amendment grounds for restricting classroom discussion of strikes. In 2020, after years of organizing, CFA helped secure passage of AB 1460, the landmark law making Ethnic Studies a graduation requirement across the CSU system — a major victory for racial justice and educational equity in one of the nation’s most racially and ethnically diverse states. Since then, it has continued fighting CSU over its implementation, defending faculty control over curriculum and the integrity of Ethnic Studies programs.

Now, at the bargaining table, CFA is seeking protections against retaliation for faculty speech, assembly, and protest through an academic freedom article that would make those protections enforceable through the union contract.

Why are state agencies and outside political organizations seeking access to the networks through which workers organize political solidarity?

The Free Press article published names and private union messages, exposing faculty, particularly faculty of color vulnerable around employment and tenure, to potential retaliation. Among those identified was Omar Zahzah, whose scholarship includes the book Terms of Servitude, on U.S. technology companies and Israeli settler colonialism. He had also recently written about the “Michigan 8,” warning of “a broader targeting of the pro-Palestine movement.” Whatever the intent, the chilling message is clear: Continue this scholarship, political writing, or union organizing, and you, too, risk public exposure and targeting.

The consequences of this attack reach into union democracy itself: Fear of exposure changes what members dare to say, whom they trust, and how they are willing to organize together. In 2025, CFA sued CSU after Cal State LA disclosed faculty and staff members’ personal contact information to federal investigators conducting an antisemitism inquiry. The union secured a January 2026 settlement requiring CSU to notify employees before complying with any specified federal demands for personal information, unless legally prohibited.

The exposure of CFA’s internal deliberations raises a question beyond leaked communications: Why are state agencies and outside political organizations seeking access to the networks through which workers organize political solidarity? In Minnesota and Michigan, that scrutiny has taken a more coercive form: undercover surveillance and federal subpoenas.

In Minnesota, federal agents infiltrated political meetings and activist chats under “Operation Puppet Master,” a surveillance operation exposed during the prosecution of the “Minnesota 15,” activists charged with conspiracy to impede federal officers. A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) slide titled “The Conspiracy” mapped 18 organizations, including unions, while Homeland Security Investigations used administrative subpoenas — requiring no judicial approval — to obtain years of financial records connected to Service Employees International Union (SEIU) and Communications Workers of America (CWA). Defense attorney Kevin Riach challenged the surveillance as lacking any “articulable criminal predicate” and violating constitutional protections; federal prosecutors maintained that the charges concerned criminal conduct alone.

At a February workers’ assembly at Minneapolis’s United Labor Centre, roughly 400 workers debated labor’s response to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). One undercover agent reported “no real threats”; another sought to “get phone numbers.” Defense attorneys are seeking federal surveillance reports, undercover device downloads, and communications between local prosecutors and Washington to establish the extent of infiltration and whether anti-ICE activists were selectively prosecuted.

Defense attorneys are seeking federal surveillance reports, undercover device downloads, and communications between local prosecutors and Washington to establish the extent of infiltration.

In Michigan, following the indictment of the Michigan 8 — eight Palestine solidarity activists accused of conspiracy — a federal grand jury subpoena demanded Graduate Employees’ Organization (GEO) records dating to January 1, 2023: current and former membership information, officers, meeting minutes, personnel, and finances.

GEO President Hiab Teshome faced felony embezzlement and false-pretenses charges over alleged misuse of student organization funds. University police also sought to bar her from campus, potentially excluding a member of the union’s bargaining team from her workplace. Both charges were dismissed on August 6 — the day the federal subpoena was signed. GEO denounced the prosecution as politically motivated and moved to quash the subpoena. The dismissal does not establish a political motive behind the federal investigation, but the juxtaposition is striking: The charges against one union leader collapsed, yet federal scrutiny extended to the entire union — who belonged to GEO, who led it, what its members discussed, and how they spent their money.

Those records could reveal how solidarity was organized. Meanwhile, GEO says university management struck proposed contract language barring disclosure of workers’ union membership to the federal government. The constitutional stakes are hardly new: In the 1958 case of NAACP v. Alabama, the Supreme Court recognized that compelled disclosure of membership lists can expose people to retaliation and deter lawful political association.

Membership lists, meeting minutes, financial records, and private communications reveal who organizes with whom. Historian Ellen Schrecker identifies a disturbing historical precedent in McCarthyism’s system of “guilt by association”: Private groups compiled dossiers, government investigated political affiliations, and employers and universities imposed punishment. She sees today’s assault on higher education as even more dire: “Today, what’s happening is worse, so much worse that we have to really find a new phrase for it,” she told Democracy Now!.

Labor has its own answer to “guilt by association”: solidarity by association — where association is not a risk to be feared, but a means of repairing what injustice or oppression has torn apart. In the words of the Minnesota 15 solidarity campaign, “Community Is Not Conspiracy.” Rather than accept the social hierarchies that divide and oppress workers, union organizers build relationships that can dismantle and transform them. In organizing with those under attack, workers discover capacities for collective action that none could exercise alone. An injury to an immigrant family facing deportation, a Black community confronting police violence, or Palestinians facing repression thus becomes a concern for workers beyond those immediately targeted.

“An injury to one is an injury to all” means little if solidarity becomes competitive or selective — if defending Jewish workers requires silence about Palestinians, if defending citizens means abandoning undocumented workers, or if wages are labor’s concern while police violence, deportations, and attacks on civil liberties belong to somebody else.

Workers need room to reflect, make mistakes and acknowledge them, disagree, organize, persuade one another, and make collective decisions without employers, the state, or outside political organizations dictating the limits of debate.

Union meetings, caucuses, and other forms of association create spaces where workers connect economic and political struggles, building solidarity across sectors rather than dividing struggles against racism, gender oppression, political repression, and exploitation into separate constituencies. Through these relationships, workers build collective power, expanding their capacity to think, feel, and act together beyond the narrow and isolated roles assigned to them in the workplace and, more broadly, under capitalism.

Yet none of this is possible without preserving unions’ internal democracy and political independence. Workers need room to reflect, make mistakes and acknowledge them, disagree, organize, persuade one another, and make collective decisions without employers, the state, or outside political organizations dictating the limits of debate. Pressfare undermines that democracy when unproven allegations and internal deliberations become material for public targeting; lawfare erodes the independence of unions when accusations and investigations impose political costs before wrongdoing is established. Undercover agents mapping worker assemblies and prosecutors demanding years of union records bring far greater coercive power to bear on those same democratic spaces.

These methods differ in form and intensity, but they reproduce the same political effects: fear, suspicion, sadness, and isolation. These are effects that weaken the relationships through which workers might act together and change their circumstances. Solidarity, by contrast, nurtures compassion, courage, and the joy of gathering in assemblies, discovering what we can accomplish together. It strengthens our capacity not only to resist oppression and exploitation but to transform the social relations that sustain them. Perhaps that is what those who fear organized labor solidarity find most threatening.

Texas’ rapidly growing data center industry could reverse much of the state’s progress on air quality by the end of the decade, according to a new report released Tuesday.

The air emissions report published by the Houston Advanced Research Center revealed that the industry’s impact on air quality depends heavily on how data centers are powered. The outlook is far worse if the facilities rely on natural gas plants.

“What we are showcasing here is that there is a significant increase in different pollutant emissions that needs to be addressed because otherwise this could have strong implications for the population and environment,” said Carlos Gamarra, vice president for energy, air and IT for HARC, whose team produced the air quality impact scenarios.

Between 2002 and 2024, Texas sharply cut its major air pollutants — particularly from transportation, industry and the power generation sectors — even as the state’s population grew by millions and its economy roughly doubled, according to the report, which used federal and state agencies’ data on air emissions.

Anthropic, one of the major industry leaders in the development of artificial intelligence (AI), has proposed legislation for Congress that would provide a framework for regulating the technology, with strict limits on which government agencies can halt AI models, and narrow conditions under which regulation can occur.

Details of the proposal, which was not initially made public, were reported on Friday by Politico.

The bill would allow the federal government to block the release or continued operation of an AI model only if it poses an imminent risk. That risk, the proposal insists, must equal either $1 billion in financial damages or the possibility of AI modeling killing or seriously injuring at least 50 people.

The risk must also be specifically tied to the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model escaping its developers’ controls, or a cyberattack of some kind.

Independent evaluators, operating under the purview of the Commerce Department, would determine if conditions exist that warrant the halting of an AI model. AI labs themselves could potentially pay the salaries of these evaluators, creating a conflict of interest within the process.

title: SCOTUS Is Undermining the Rules That Have Kept US Elections Peaceful for Decades
content:
The Roberts Court has dismantled guardrails preventing a president from turning state agencies against political rivals.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Courts can create violence simply by putting words on paper. For anyone who has examined any legal system, this should not be a controversial proposition. Some observers argue that the very purpose of written judgments is to justify acts of violence. But one need not go that far to see the immediate effects: A judicial opinion can cause a death, ignite a civil war, legitimize a coup, or even wipe out an entire culture.

If we accept that basic truth, it should not surprise us that jurisprudence can also fuel election-related violence. In U.S. history, the most salient example is United States v. Cruikshank, an all-but-forgotten Reconstruction-era ruling. In Cruikshank, the Supreme Court held that the federal government could not prosecute the broad-daylight massacre of dozens of Black Republicans in 1873, most of whom were defending political offices duly won by their candidates. After two grueling trials and an unlikely guilty verdict by a Louisiana jury, the Court threw out the convictions.

On Saturday, France saw its largest nationwide protests in years, as popular outrage over the rising cost of living converged with a month-long student movement against the country’s neglected public education system.

Nearly 800,000 people took to the streets in over 140 cities across France on Saturday, according to France’s major labor union, the CGT. The protests were made up of high school and university students who have blockaded their schools over the past month, demanding better education conditions, as well as labor unions, who mobilized workers in protest of public service cuts, and remnants of the 2018 “Yellow Vests” movement.

Mass protests during the day transformed into riots as evening fell, with multiple city halls and offices set ablaze or otherwise damaged. Police arrested some 2,400 protesters.

French leaders have placed blame on the protesters and the far left, including on the far left political party La France Insoumise (LFI), or France Unbowed. A 56-year-old Mexican man held at a federal immigration facility in Laredo was found dead in his cell Saturday morning, his daughter and U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Laredo, confirmed to The Texas Tribune.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unresponsive by staff at the Rio Grande Processing Center during a security check at around 10 a.m. Saturday, Cuellar said. Staff performed CPR and called emergency services.

Andrade-Covarrubias is the seventh person to die while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas this year — the first being Geraldo Lunas Campos, whose death was ruled a homicide by the El Paso Medical Examiner’s office in January.

He’s also the second to die in an ICE facility in Laredo this year. Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, a 63-year-old Mexican who was being held at Webb County Detention Center, died on June 19 after being found unresponsive, according to the agency.

The GEO Group, which operates the facility, referred the Tribune to ICE. Officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent Sunday and Monday.

Kathy Hochul (who is running for re-election in New York), features her walking alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. title: Aging Coal Plants Turn Into a Midterm Fight Over Energy Costs

Climate and energy battles are running through campaigns in Michigan, Colorado, Indiana, and beyond.

Craig Unit 1, a coal-fired power plant distinguished by tall exhaust smokestacks that rise above a rolling landscape in northwestern Colorado, was scheduled to close for good at the end of 2025 amid pressure from environmental advocates, public interest groups and state officials.

But on Dec. 30, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered it to keep burning coal. The unit had suffered a mechanical failure 11 days earlier and was not even running. Wright has since renewed the order three times — most recently on Sept. 25, extending the plant’s life through Christmas Day, a full year past its retirement date.

Its operator, Tri-State Generation and Transmission, is a nonprofit rural cooperative, and in January it joined co-owner Platte River Power Authority, a public power agency, in arguing that Wright’s orders violate the Constitution and federal law — a fight that has since reached a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. Kamora Greggs returned to her college campus with voting on her mind. She’d just visited her home in Jackson, Mississippi, about three hours away, when her mom encouraged her to exercise her right.

“And don’t have anybody change your mind about what you want to do,” Greggs recalled.

As a first time voter, the 19-year-old health and kinesiology major wanted to know more about the process, the role of government, and hear directly from her peers about why they thought voting is important.

She and dozens of other Coahoma Community College students participated in a September town hall – playing games like Levels, learning history and the power of the ballot box — at their school in Clarksdale.

“It’s a good way to learn with your friends,” Greggs said. “It really impacted me and made me want to actually get out there and spread the word and make sure other people my age know that it’s a good idea to get registered to vote.”

title: My Study of Dystopian Fiction Never Prepared Me for Reality Here in Gaza
