As a 27-year-old English literature graduate and English teacher from Gaza, I have always been passionate about teaching. I enjoy helping my students learn to speak English by reciting stories aloud.

I connect with them through English, so I collected every English-language book my hands could reach. Before October 7, 2023, during my fourth year in university, I used to visit a bookshop in Gaza City to buy English novels for enhancing my linguistic link with my job and the students. In 2022, shortly before I graduated, I wrote a short story about our tough conditions in Gaza and submitted it to a writing competition. It ranked seventh out of 80 stories, and I received a reward. What began as a practice to improve my English turned into a way of life. Whenever I had money, I bought a few novels until I gathered a large collection and built my own English library. Sometimes I purchased novels I would never open, but it felt satisfying to have them on my shelf. I could sense linguistic progress: a future.

More than 100,000 Ukrainians and roughly 2,000 Sudanese immigrants are bracing for the possibility they’ll lose their humanitarian protections by Monday.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has not indicated if he will renew protections for Ukrainians, who first received Temporary Protected Status after Russia invaded their country in 2022, and for Sudanese nationals, who were granted the designation several times, most recently in 2022, because of an ongoing civil war.

The Trump administration has moved to eliminate legal protections for more than 1 million immigrants that have TPS. Of the 17 countries with the designation at the start of the second Trump administration, the only remaining protections are for Ukraine and Sudan, which are set to end on Monday, and Lebanon, which is set to expire Nov. 27.

Mullin is supposed to declare his decision at least 60 days before a TPS designation expires, but he’s made no announcement.

Oil and gas companies will now be permitted to kill polar bears and Pacific walruses off the northern coast of Alaska so long as such killings are “unintentional,” according to a new Trump administration rule.

The US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) on Friday finalized a rule change that would shield fossil fuel companies from legal liability if they engage in the “incidental, unintentional” killing of the animals “during year-round oil and gas industry activities in the Beaufort Sea… and adjacent northern coast of Alaska.”

Under the rule change, which is scheduled to last through 2031, the FWS “will issue letters of authorization” that sign off on the incidental killing of wildlife upon request by oil and gas companies.

As noted by a report in Bloomberg Law, the proposed rule change “drew more than 85,500 public comments, nearly all in opposition,” before the FWS ultimately signed off on it.

The rule change was a major priority for the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, which represents fossil fuel giants and requested the revision in September 2025.

title: As Trump Sabotages the ICC With Sanctions, There Are Many Ways to Fight Back

The U.S. government has long sought to incapacitate the International Criminal Court (ICC), the world’s first global court that was created to prosecute the most atrocious crimes. As the ICC seeks to provide accountability for Israeli crimes, the Trump administration has become increasingly aggressive in its attempts to hobble the court. On October 9, 2026, Team Trump imposed punitive sanctions against the court itself, which constitutes the gravest intensification of its war on the ICC. But there are several strategies available to mitigate the worst effects of these sanctions.

In February 2025, Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14203, which authorizes the imposition of sanctions against the ICC. The sanctions amount to illegal unilateral coercive measures because only the UN Security Council has the authority to impose sanctions.

The executive order prohibits U.S. persons from providing material support or services to certain designated persons and entities, including financial services. title: Trump Admin Just Effectively Killed a Popular Renewable Energy Program
content:
Solar panels can be an economic lifeline in the rural US — but now they’re going to be a lot harder to build.

Earlier this month, after a series of stops and starts, the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced changes to a long-running program that is supposed to help farmers and rural small businesses stand up renewable energy projects.

Abdul-Rahman al-Nashash, 11, holds onto the edge of a chair and pushes his left leg into a plastic prosthetic that doesn’t fit him anymore. The bone that was cut two years ago has kept growing inside, and it presses painfully against his skin.

His doctors told him to stop wearing it. He wears it anyway, every morning, pulling the straps tight and rolling his pants down so no one sees the plastic before he takes his first step. He bites his lip when it hurts and holds his shoulders straight so no one can tell he is limping.

“He forces himself to wear it,” his mother said, “just so no one knows he has a disability.”

Before the genocide, al-Nashash played for a local soccer club, and he would chase the ball across a dirt field until the sun went down. He is the eldest son in his family, and he was the one his mother leaned on at home. When she needed water, he was the one who ran to carry the heavy gallon of water, and he never got tired. Now, he is not able.

When he finally takes the prosthetic off, he sits curled up. He is waiting for his third surgery, and his mother said he will need one every year.

The Postal Service has lost money for decades. Since 2007, the agency has lost $118 billion. Things are so bad that the Postmaster General has warned that the agency could run out of cash early next year.

Doctors in outbreak areas are making changes to how they care for pregnant patients and their babies, offering a glimpse of what may be in store across the nation as cases spread.

Among the deaths were two infants in Lancaster County, an area about 60 miles west of Philadelphia and the epicenter of the Pennsylvania outbreak. A newborn had congenital measles, which was passed in utero through an unvaccinated mother who was infected. It is not clear whether the other infant, who was reportedly 6 weeks old at the time of death and had a genetic birth disorder, was exposed in utero or after birth.

Some Pennsylvania-based doctors have experienced an uptick in anxious questions from patients about the implications of measles on just about all aspects of pregnancy care: What do more cases mean for a current pregnancy? title: Indigenous People Are Resisting Erasure From Schools, Media, and Our Land
content:

On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas that the Indigenous Lucayan people called Guanahani. He continued on to Cuba and Hispaniola and, on later voyages, to other parts of the Caribbean, but he never set foot in what is now the continental United States. It makes little sense for a country to honor a man who never reached it, and even less to credit him with discovering a place that millions of people already called home. And it makes even less given what Columbus actually did in the places where he stepped foot: He rounded up Indigenous people in the Caribbean, chained them, and sent them as slaves to Spain. And when Indigenous communities rose up in resistance, he ordered his soldiers to “spread terror,” maiming and slaughtering civilians en masse using firearms, dogs, swords, and pikes.

But despite all this, in 1937, the United States established a federal holiday in his name anyway.

Warm Springs remains in recovery, but grassroots organizers who grew up on the reservation have managed to remedy some of the crisis during and after the fire through mutual aid and direct action.

title: Extreme Weather Disasters Cost Hundreds of Billions. Let’s Make Polluters Pay.
content:

One of the most visible consequences of global warming is the increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, such as the powerful nor’easter that hammered the East Coast and mid-Atlantic for several days in late September with heavy rain, winds, and flooding. Indeed, a wide array of scientific studies over the past couple of decades have shown how human-caused climate change affects the intensity, frequency, and impact of extreme weather — from wildfires in the U.S. and Australia to record-setting flooding in China. And now, a major study prepared by two dozen scientists from across the globe has found a link between industrial emissions and the warming of the snow-capped Himalayan region that led to the collapse of the glacier that caused the catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet last month, in which over 1,300 people were killed while thousands are still missing.

title: I Carry the Key to My Destroyed Home in Gaza to Keep Alive My Dream of Returning
content:
The word “ceasefire” entered the news on October 11, 2025, but it has still not entered our lives as a reality.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

On the night of March 18, 2025, while we were observing Ramadan, my family and I woke to the sound of very loud explosions, one after another.

We all woke up frightened and began asking my father, “What happened? Has the war returned?”

My father did not answer. No one knew anything.

We stayed together, waiting for morning, not knowing what was happening.

We had not expected the first ceasefire to be broken. We had already spent nearly a year living through war, and we had been looking forward to Ramadan with the hope that it would come without the bombing and fear.

The first ceasefire in Gaza had lasted nearly two months before Israel resumed its airstrikes that day, ending the period of relative calm that had begun on January 19, 2025.

Then everything became quiet. We ate suhoor, the early morning meal eaten before the daily fast of Ramadan begins, we prayed Fajr (the pre-dawn prayer), and went back to sleep.

But we were overwhelmed by grief and exhaustion. We loved Ramadan, and we had been waiting for it for a whole year, hoping that it would finally be a time to feel some happiness after a year of displacement, hunger, war, and exhaustion.

Together, they accounted for more than $678 million — or more than a third of the outside spending by 794 groups tracked by OpenSecrets, and a sum nearly equal to the combined spending of the next 34 groups. Each of those groups serves a distinct purpose. For example, the Senate Leadership Fund works to elect Republicans to the Senate while the Congressional Leadership Fund does the same for the GOP’s House candidates and WinSenate PAC supports Democrats running for Senate seats. title: A Shadow of Fear Hangs Over Gazans Amid Israeli Defense Minister’s Threats
content:
Israel Katz says Israel will forcibly displace 1 million Gazans if “even one Israeli soldier” is abducted.

We are about to close out three years and enter another since Israel invaded Gaza, but we are not leaving the war behind to begin a new life. We are entering yet another year without knowing when this war will end — or whether it will end at all.

The fear remains. The destruction remains. The threats remain. It feels as though each passing year does not bring us closer to an end, but closer to the possibility of another war.

Despite everything we are living through in Gaza, we understand what it means to live one day at a time — to hold on to every simple moment we can still have. Imagine planning for another morning, perhaps for the simplest of things: going out with the friends you still have, or taking your family to the sea in the morning, amid all this destruction, simply to experience a moment that feels like life.

Then, as you are planning that ordinary morning, you hear a statement from Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, who said on September 22: “If even one Israeli soldier or civilian is abducted, the city of Gaza — with its homes and terrorist towers — will be evacuated southward of its one million residents.”

Each year, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which is primarily responsible for implementing the law, evaluates species and lists them as “endangered” or “threatened.” When federal activity or private development has the potential to harm a listed species or its habitat, project developers are required to consult with the Service or obtain a permit prior to construction.

When I left Gaza in 2024, after six months of living through genocide, I wanted one thing above all else: to spare my only child a life spent permanently at war. I did not want him to grow up believing that the whole world looked like Gaza.

But I left more than fifteen nieces and nephews behind. Many were still too young to understand the world they had been born into. They were learning what a home was, what a school was, what it meant to be alive, at the very moment those things were being destroyed around them.

I spent the next year and a half in Cairo. It took me a long time to learn how to inhabit ordinary life again. Whenever I saw a garden, a playground, a school, or children playing freely and safely in the street, I could not simply enjoy the sight. Gaza was always there, beneath it.

A garden brought back the rubble. A school brought back the children who no longer had one. Even safety became a reminder of those still denied it.

A competing GOP bill creates legal guardrails for police when using ALPR data but would not “ban” license plate surveillance by the federal government.

Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year — nearly four times the amount of cases recorded across the entire U.S. in 2024.

The Keystone State has recorded 198 hospitalizations and five deaths as a result of the ongoing measles outbreak.

On Monday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) declared an emergency order in New York, citing the rising number of measles cases in neighboring states, including Pennsylvania, and an increase in cases in rural areas.

The move comes as the total number of measles cases across the U.S. this year has reached 4,020, according to figures collected by Johns Hopkins University. Aside from Pennsylvania, Texas and South Carolina are also at or near the 1,000-cases mark.

There haven’t been this many cases of measles in the U.S. since the early 1990s.

The current numbers mark a significant departure from the number of cases seen just a few years ago. content:
The factors show how easily another failed execution could occur, even as others are planned soon in Texas and Florida.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Over the course of two hours, witnesses watched and listened as Christa Pike cried, whimpered and snored through Tennessee’s attempt to execute her. By the end of it, executioners had given her two doses of the state’s lethal injection drugs. Her arms were swollen and blistered, and one had turned purple, her attorneys said. And she was still alive, marking what legal experts say is the first time a prisoner in the U.S. has survived one dose — let alone two — of lethal injection drugs.

Even if the outcome was unprecedented, what went wrong was not. Pike’s was the third Tennessee execution in 14 months to go awry. But as a reporter who has covered death row for nearly a decade and witnessed several executions, I know the state is not alone. The factors behind the breakdowns in Tennessee have popped up again and again across the country — and show how easily another botched execution could occur, even as soon as the ones planned Wednesday in Texas and next week in Florida.

An ICE traffic stop that year in Detroit landed Lucia in detention, just weeks after her partner was also detained by ICE.

Lucia was transferred to four different detention centers before arriving at the South Louisiana Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana. She described her time there as “horrible.”

The USDA, which oversees the U.S. Forest Service, initially gave the public only 30 days to comment on the plan. They were forced after public pressure to allow 15 additional days, until October 6. Opponents are aiming to mobilize 1 million public comments during this short period, as well as sponsoring public events speaking out against the repeal.

One hundred and eighty environmental, conservation, and citizen’s groups have been joined by tribes, sportsmen, wildland firefighters, and businesses dedicated to tourism, in submitting a joint public comment or otherwise speaking out against this decision. title: Maryland Used Discredited Science to Convict a Woman of Murdering Her Newborn
content:

Moira Akers was prosecuted and convicted of the murder of a newborn in 2022. She claims to have given birth to a stillborn baby in her home in Columbia, Maryland, in 2018.

Prosecutors doubted Akers’ story, using her online searches for abortion services and lack of prenatal care as evidence of ill intent. But it was a “forensic method” devised in the 17th century that proved key to Akers’ conviction.

The method, known as a “float test,” was designed to determine if a baby was stillborn or born alive by placing the lungs of a deceased fetus in water. If the lungs float, then they are aerated, meaning the baby was breathing and alive prior to their death.

In 2018, former Maryland chief medical examiner Dr. David Fowler signed the autopsy report that, using the float test as proof, determined that Akers’ baby died after Akers asphyxiated it. Fowler also testified in Akers’ trial. Prosecutors used Fowler’s testimony and autopsy report as evidence to convict Akers of second-degree murder in 2022.

I grew up walking the boardwalk in downtown Wilmington, North Carolina, peering into the froth of the Cape Fear River. The name came from 16th-century mariners who feared its mouth, which was known to churn ships into wrecks. But for the last few decades, there has been something new to fear in the river.

The Cape Fear River was tainted with per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), the Wilmington Star-News reported in 2017, a group of synthetic compounds now commonly known as “forever chemicals.”

As their name suggests, forever chemicals are renowned for their persistence. One of the strongest bonds in chemistry, carbon and fluorine, gives PFAS their nonstick properties. A seemingly endless list of products — dental floss, tampons, cellphones, wall paint, yoga pants, carpets, contact lenses, hair-straightening treatments, toilet paper — rely on those bonds to smooth, harden, slicken, and withstand heat and wear. title: Alito Reverses Course, Announces Recusal From Major Corporate Fossil Fuels Case
content:
The Supreme Court associate justice had previously refused to step away from a case involving fossil fuel companies.

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito is recusing himself from a climate crisis-related case before the court this year, reversing his previous announcement that he would remain on the case despite his personal financial interests in its outcome.

Clerk of Court Scott Harris sent the announcement to attorneys on both sides of the pending matter on Monday.

“I am writing to inform the parties that Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case,” Harris wrote.

The letter gave no explanation as to why Alito came to the decision to recuse himself.

The case features ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy, which are seeking to have a Colorado-based lawsuit against them dropped, citing federal law they claim supersedes state statutes. State municipalities are suing the companies, seeking to hold them financially liable for the impacts of the climate crisis.

Alito does not have any financial stakes in either company. However, the associate justice does hold stocks in other fossil fuel-based companies, which means the outcome of the case could still directly benefit him.

title: ICE Is Still Targeting the Haitian Community in Springfield
content:
Hundreds of Haitians in Springfield are being forced to wear ankle monitors while they await immigration hearings.

For the past two months, hundreds of Haitians in Springfield have been targeted by immigration authorities and forced to wear ankle monitors, as the Trump administration metes out collective punishment to appeal to its far right base.

Since the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians at the end of June, immigration enforcement has ramped up its detentions and deportations of Haitians — with its surge most concentrated in Springfield, Ohio.

The overturn of TPS was followed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sending letters to Haitian immigrants in Springfield, requiring them to report in person so they could be fitted with ankle monitors to track their locations until it is decided whether they will be deported. Throughout August, ICE’s surveillance of Haitians in Springfield through ankle monitors continued to rise.

Michaelle Louis, a Haitian organizer in Springfield, spoke with Truthout about the effects of the ankle monitoring program on members of her community.
